en: The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness of the Sublime Dharma, Scroll One.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master and State Preceptor of the Western Heaven (India), Magadha Province in Central India, Nālandā Monastery, during the Great Song Dynasty; conferred the rank of "Purple Robe."
The Śramaṇa臣 (Official) Fǎtiān, in obedience to the Imperial Decree, translated: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was amidst a great assembly, surrounded by devas and humans, who gazed upon his venerable countenance, their eyes never for a moment wavering.
Then, the great assembly spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"We take refuge in the All-Knowing One, The Supreme Honored One of the three worlds,
Who spreads forth subtle and wondrous sounds, Bringing vast benefit to all living beings."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly and spoke in verse:
"If there are sentient beings who do not kill and bestow fearlessness,
Who possess a compassionate heart and are able to endure with patience, They shall be upright and dignified, with a lifespan beyond compare."
If, toward sentient beings, one regards them as one’s own parents, one can abstain from taking what is not given; such wisdom and merit are immeasurable.
If one performs wholesome physical actions with a firm mind free from desire, [the merit is likewise vast].
Not beholding the exquisite forms of women, one is liberated from the evil realms.
The world should be shunned; liberation is joyfully to be realized.
Like gold ore concealed within its covering, the essential nature is fundamentally pure.
Afflictions cannot be subdued; one craves exquisite tactile sensations.
Failing to distinguish between good and evil deeds, the suffering of this fleeting life is greatest.
Suffering and pleasure arise from the mind; the same applies to gain and loss.
The association with or separation from good and evil friends, and the principle of cause and effect, are without partiality.
To subdue the disorder of the sensory faculties, to practice with a mind of equanimity,
and to benefit all sentient beings— this is called the conduct of a bhikṣu.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, you must subdue and sever the afflictions;
cultivate and increase wisdom, and keep the mind from distraction.
You must realize the principle of nirvāṇa and distance yourselves from all suffering.
Diligently cultivate the mind of right view; the Buddha has said this is beyond compare!
It liberates one from all saṃsāra; like Mount Sumeru, it is unmoved by craving, equal to the fragrance of sandalwood, and its nectar-like flavor is peerless.
Though receiving the highest offerings—fine garments of kauseya and exquisite silk—he is not stained by craving or attachment; content, his heart is joyful.
Like grass consumed by fire, he understands that such things are not ultimate.
By making offerings, one increases merit and wisdom; neither water nor fire can invade such a person.
This is the fruit of pure karma and true knowledge; like the waters of a river, it is never exhausted.
Not craving any sensory realms—this, the Buddha said, is the practice of a bhikṣu.
Seeking various forms of wisdom, may they be constantly present in accordance with it;
realizing the true nature of phenomena, may they not fall into the cycles of saṃsāra.
If a person seeks the pure dharmas, they should keep the mind from becoming distracted.
Bestowing grace upon all realms, it cannot be destroyed even by the fires at the end of an eon.
Ignorance is the root of all existence; from this, the cycle of rebirth arises.
Diligently subduing and eliminating afflictions—this is the true practice of a Muni.
Delighting in the practice of patience, upright and free from enmity or harm,
the cause of the Sage’s wondrous marks brings joy to the hearts of all who behold him.
In forest glades free from clamor, he dwells with a mind full of love and joy.
Carrying the alms-bowl and always taking but one meal—this is called the practice of a bhikṣu.
Liberation is the supreme bliss; the three miserable realms are the greatest suffering.
True Suchness is free from "this" and "that," and cannot be apprehended through conceptual thought.
His actions for the benefit of others are impartial; he is gentle, ever-sincere, and his right conduct is constantly in accord with reality, remaining far removed from all false attachments.
The faculty of mind delights in grasping, and thus the faculty of mind is called the most preeminent.
The faculty of mind is swift; the faculty of mind is joyful.
This is proclaimed in verse: it can act and it can speak;
it shakes off all afflictions and thoroughly understands the fruits of karma.
Fully understanding matters of gain and loss, one is able to proceed toward sublime enlightenment;
among all sentient beings, such a person is foremost among those with the six sense faculties.
Delighting in dwelling within the forest, they remain far removed from all enemies and thieves.
Having thoroughly understood these six sense faculties, right practice emerges from them.
Constantly abiding in the state of meditative equipoise, one shakes off all karmic obstructions;
just as in the sky, wind and clouds cannot defile it.
Well-guarding body, speech, and mind, Always in accord with right view,
With wisdom like the light of a lamp, The hosts of Māra cannot destroy them.
Non-harming of beings is called "wholesome"; compassion and altruism are profound.
When one's deportment is free from transgressions, only then does the mind of a bhikṣu abide.
The eye is bound by the realm of forms; obstructed by these, it does not turn toward anything else.
Afflictions bind sentient beings, preventing them from escaping the three realms.
The wisdom of the ultimate and the conventional is subtle;
its skillful application is rare and praised by all Buddhas alike, its functioning beyond the reach of thought.
"Though one seeks liberation through much learning, greed and anger cannot be overcome;
therefore, well-guarding the three karmas of the body, one must subdue and eliminate them so they do not arise.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:

"If there are sentient beings bound by afflictions, transmigrating through the three realms and undergoing various sufferings and vexations, yet who practice the ten wholesome deeds and thereby experience the fruits of rebirth among humans and devas, they will feel love, joy, and delight."
It is like the full moon, free from all obstructions and incomparably pure, which brings joy to those who behold it;

or like fire, which can burn wood and fuel—so too should these evil karmas be subdued and eliminated, so that one may leave behind the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and be liberated from all suffering;
or like a bird that has escaped its bonds, moving with sovereign ease and without hindrance.

If all sentient beings were not to create karma, they would transcend the three realms and realize the principle of the two emptinesses; they would not be invaded by suffering and affliction, nor stained by greed and anger, and would fully comprehend the nature of saṃsāra.

Just as the light of a lamp clearly illuminates forms and images, so too is right wisdom ever-present and uninterrupted; free from all false attachments, one delights in tranquility, abandons all evils among tombs and beneath trees, and draws near to virtuous friends.
In this way, a bhikṣu cultivates the practice of renunciation; he should not be greedily attached to any desirable objects or sensory realms.
He takes no pleasure in dwellings, avoids trade and false speech, and finds no delight in song or dance. Having abandoned both hatred and attachment, he eats but one meal a day in the forest.

He constantly seeks to attain supreme bodhi, refrains from taking what is not given, wears robes of discarded rags with joy and contentment, and dwells in the wilderness in silent contemplation, free from distracted thoughts, greed, anger, and the like.

Constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, remaining far removed from the darkness of ignorance while cultivating wisdom; free from the karma of afflictions and liberated from birth and death, one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, brings about the manifestation of tranquility, and destroys all afflictions and sufferings.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should cultivate firm roots of goodness, distance yourselves from defiled desires, and focus the mind on a single object with delight in *tathatā*.
May various forms of wisdom increase, fulfilling the untainted pure dharmas, and thoroughly understand that tainted phenomena are illusory and unreal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If there is a bhikṣu who abides in the holy life (brahmacarya), who is pure and gentle, who has skillfully cultivated śamatha and vipaśyanā, who delights in meditative concentration (dhyāna), who sports in the forest, who remains far removed from all defilements, and who thoroughly understands delusion—such a one is like a flying bird whose shadow follows it through the sky."

The bhikṣu is likewise: keeping the three robes upon his person, he skillfully cultivates equanimity; constantly contemplating the True Dharma to subdue and extinguish afflictions, he accords with wisdom, seeks the Path of Vision, and proceeds even unto the further shore, ultimate nirvāṇa.
Monks, you should know that by observing in this way and dwelling in joy, you shall always stand in awe of saṃsāra, as well as of old age, sickness, and death.
Just as the asuras and other celestial hosts, with joy and reverence, obtain exquisite saṃghāṭī robes and alms bowls without needing any other vessels;
so too, you must guard the holy life (brahmacarya) so as not to let it be violated, remaining pure and stainless, unattached to flavors or gain and honor.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If sentient beings abandon the mind of compassion, becoming arrogant and negligent, they will burn away all roots of goodness and find it difficult to exhaust all outflows."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one abandons compassionate diligence, And remains associated with ignorance and pride,
Tranquility will not manifest, And there is no means by which outflows can be extinguished."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Furthermore, if there is anyone who possesses bedding and requisites that are most excellent, fine, and soft, they should not take pleasure in them."
Awakening to the fact that ignorance is the root of delusion and darkness, all various afflictions arise accordingly;

it is said that this ignorance pervades all defiled minds, for if it were absent, one would not be deluded or darkened, would thoroughly comprehend all phenomena, would abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dhyāna, and would exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
Thereupon the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If you wish to practice walking meditation, do so in the forest in a state of stillness and without distraction; you should not take delight in unwholesome states or in objects such as alcohol, women, and the like."
"Monk, it is thus: if the hosts of Māras, bound by karma, disturb one who cultivates goodness, it is like a person who drinks poison and must suffer the consequences themselves;
you now break the precepts and practice wrong livelihood, bound by afflictions, and shall fall into the great hells to undergo various sufferings."
“Bhikṣus, you should know: when going on almsround, if you see a woman, regard her as a venomous snake;

concentrate your mind one-pointedly to contemplate the True Dharma, seeking neither fame nor profit nor various exquisite sensory objects; free yourself from the bonds of karma so that the mind becomes equanimous, and do not engage in slander.”
When entering a village, one should maintain the perception of it as a forest wilderness;
when begging for food and drink, one should maintain the perception of treating an illness;
and when afflictions arise, one should maintain the perception of burning down a forest.
When seeking the sublime Dharma, one should maintain the perception of treading upon the right path;
when reclining on a bed, the perception of being startled by a deer;
and when entering various meditative absorptions, the perception of wandering through a garden.
Upon seeing an Arhat, one should regard them as a field of merit.
One should take no pleasure in sensory objects, speech, or frivolous conceptual proliferation, but constantly seek liberation.
Even when kings, ministers, or relatives approach for their benefit and offer exquisite food and drink, one must not harbor thoughts of longing or greed.
The donors seek fame and profit, yet they are never deceitful; in their mental conduct they employ skillful means and do not give rise to anger.

Craving pleasure in dwellings, they associate with the powerful and noble families like fish delighting in water; they remain settled therein without relinquishing it. They distance themselves from true spiritual friends and turn their backs on reality, seeking after the illusory—like a lamp, a dream, or lightning—while imagining this to be liberation.
"Respecting false paths and constantly practicing reverence, they are unable to realize the supreme truth.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know and be mindful; delight in walking meditation, dhyāna-concentration, and wisdom; constantly practice a heart of loving-kindness, and strive to seek the supreme, true liberation."
Having attained right view and thoroughly understood all phenomena, they constantly cultivate patience and diligence, and abandon greed, anger, and all forms of distraction.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"One should cherish and delight in all sentient beings, mindful of them with compassion, so as to cause them to leave behind their inversions and various fetters, and to be liberated from all suffering."
"Monks, you should know that regarding all sense objects, one must remain free from defilement and harm.
It is like the nature of gold, which is inherently free from dust and impurities.

'Bhikṣus, you should know that whether you approach a close friend or go to one who is not a friend, you should remain free from greed and anger, and clearly understand what is harmful and beneficial.'"

Whether regarding offenses or non-offenses, security or hardship, he employs skillful means to subdue them, preaching the essentials of the Dharma according to their sharp or dull faculties, their intelligence or ignorance, and guiding them toward the superior or inferior paths, admonishing them with the correct teaching.

“Bhikṣus, you should know: practice walking meditation in the forest and cultivate meditative concentration in secluded places; abandon faults and transgressions, and always delight in *tathatā* (suchness); clearly understand and believe in the distinctions between superior and inferior causes and effects;
remain far removed from all poisons and subdue the sense faculties so that no faults arise; let the mind rejoice through association with wisdom, and bring to rest all slander.”

Like the ocean, it is profoundly deep; its correspondence is inexhaustible. The mind and intellect are firm and steadfast, giving rise to no doubt. One does not crave exquisite forms, but possesses wisdom and compassion with equanimity.

One speaks well according to the occasion regarding the false and the true within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. One refrains from speaking of worldly right and wrong, remaining far removed from all states of existence that entail faults and afflictions.
Just as one would not allow various poisons or mud to cause harm, so too [this teaching] liberates one from saṃsāra and distances one from ignorance.
Through meditative concentration and wisdom, it most excellently proclaims the meaning of the Dharma with eloquence; it is free from delusion and inversion.
It allows no defilement by any dust or impurity, and all that is performed is for the sake of benefit.
Regarding the Sangha, one does not give rise to actions of body, speech, or mind that are contrary to it; being free from those fetters, one seeks neither the realms of humans nor devas;
one cultivates various wholesome deeds not for the sake of fame or profit, but for the purpose of proceeding toward Nirvana.
“Bhikṣus, you should know: always avoid evil friends and do not commit any wrongs; constantly observe all things with an impartial mind of loving-kindness;
keep the mind and intentions supple and harmonious, guard the precepts with purity, and accord with reality.”
Free from the fear of being a concubine, they are not deluded by saṃsāra or the various meditative concentrations; they have realized impermanence and attained mastery over the wisdom of emptiness.
The gods of the Brahma assembly dwell securely in meditative concentration and proceed toward nirvāṇa.
Having heard the sublime Dharma and realized its truth, they were filled with joy and exultation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The fruits of karma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, Are certain to be experienced as they were performed."
One binds oneself through one's own actions, no different from a silkworm spinning its cocoon.
Whether bitter or sweet, all sufferings and afflictions follow one constantly like a shadow; by drinking poison, one brings harm upon oneself.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there are sentient beings who skillfully cultivate wisdom, destroy the fire of afflictions, abide securely in the holy life (brahmacarya), and take delight in the Triple Gem; who rejoice upon seeing or hearing [the Dharma], give rise to no greed or anger, and conceive the thought of liberation;
who thoroughly understand the immovable and proceed toward the truth, abiding in the supreme state."
"One shall be free from old age, sickness, death, and the continuous succession of saṃsāra, afflictions, and enemies.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one cultivates the holy life in a secluded place and proceeds toward self-arisen wisdom, the hosts of devas and Brahmās will constantly come to draw near, pay homage, serve, and make offerings."

Why is this? Because delighting in the holy life (*brahmacarya*) can destroy cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); it distances one from afflictions (*kleśa*), tames the mind, and causes one to abandon darkness and all enemies so that they may not cause harm.
"Just as dry grass is separated from the fire that consumes it, so too is it with one who has abandoned the afflictions.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, if there is someone who is deluded regarding various objects, who gives free rein to the sense faculties, who turns his back on nirvāṇa, whose mind is not equanimous, who constantly performs the causes of suffering, and who is bound by wrong views such that he cannot subdue or eliminate any of the delusions; [he is like dry grass still in contact with the fire]."

Having extensively gathered the requisites for practice, their greedy minds blaze intensely; though they are the supreme fields of merit, they are obscured by ignorance and delusion, never attaining awakening.

If they encounter a Dharma Master who skillfully transforms them, they will distance themselves from all delusions and the defilements of greed, extinguish the fierce flames, and detach from all sensory contacts. Thus they shall incline toward the sublime Dharma of supreme nectar and abide in the highest state.
A virtuous friend delights in meditative concentration and cultivates wisdom; though afflictions may be as vast as mountains, they can be destroyed.
Abiding in pure wisdom, one abandons all ignorance and darkness, departs from saṃsāra, and attains sublime karmic fruition.
Possessing supreme wisdom, they cultivate all sublime practices with a continuous flow of mind.
Having few desires and being content, they extinguish and eliminate false attachments, remaining entirely free from the bonds of objective clinging.
Just as a fish swallows the hook, binding itself through its craving for flavor;

so too it is with sentient beings: delighting in the five desires, they never relinquish them, extensively generating various karmas, revolving through birth and death without cessation. Deluded by the causes of defilement, their distinctions among the various realms of existence are without end.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If a person commits evil deeds, They will revolve through the sufferings of hell,
As hungry ghosts and animals, Sinking into them without end."
Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Pratāpana, and the Avīci Great Hell; there,
through the suffering of arduous and evil karma, thorns sixteen finger-breadths long pierce them.
"The four walls and the four gates are all constructed of iron.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The flames of those hells are fiercely blazing; they are violent and numerous, continuing without interruption. Extending for hundreds of yojanas, they are difficult to subdue. Their forms cause one's hair to stand on end, inspiring great terror, and their most evil sounds cause all who hear them to feel bitter anguish."

When sentient beings fall into this hell due to their evil karma, they are positioned with heads downward and feet upward; in an instant they are born there and undergo various sufferings, being burned and scorched as they are turned over and over. Day and night they weep, emitting great cries of distress;
like fish being skewered and roasted, their skin and flesh are mangled and rotted away. Enveloped in total darkness, their minds become utterly bewildered.
When the sinners behold that realm of Yama, where great fires burn and consume all, they become bewildered and faint with distress.
Those who have committed similar karma are cast into a single prison; each person is bound and hauled about by the wardens, enduring unbearable suffering without interruption.
"If a person possesses little wisdom and falsely commits transgressions, they will cycle through existence because of this, meeting with enemies and undergoing the sufferings of hell.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How are those who undergo punishment under Yama bound, such that they experience immeasurable suffering?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"This person has constantly slandered the True Dharma and failed to give rise to faith and acceptance. Not understanding cause and effect, he is deluded regarding the various hells and feels no fear. He gives rise to the fire of afflictions, which burns away all roots of goodness."
Due to these karmic causes, one falls into the realm of Yama and undergoes such suffering; the most intense fires of calamity burn without interruption.
Hostile enemies of hatred and the darkness of ignorance are experienced in accordance with one's karma, and only when the karma is exhausted does one emerge.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, if there is a person who is deceitful, hypocritical, and fraudulent;
who indulges in and does not abandon lust for the wives and daughters of others; who is bound by fetters like one born blind, constantly shrouded from the light, and unable to attain awakening."
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one dwells in a lowly and base station, being foolish and lacking wisdom, by what further cause does one bring about such a result?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In the past, because his mind was puffed up with pride, he disparaged the virtuous and good, and was stingy, greedy, and envious; therefore, he has received this retribution."
Furthermore, if there is a person who sows discord between others and commits evil deeds, by reason of these causes and conditions, they will fall into the various hells.

If they are born among humans, they will lack sons or daughters; their wealth and possessions will be lost; their friends and associates will abandon them; and at the time when life is about to end, they will become insane and terrified.
Though their kinsmen protect them, they will be deluded regarding all sensory objects and will be unable to attain clear understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"What one does oneself, one receives back; For sentient beings who commit the crime of harming others, The instruments of suffering are violent and manifold; Only when karma is exhausted can one be released."
"When people in the world perform various deeds, whether wholesome or unwholesome, they are constantly followed by them;
just as flowers possess fragrance, it pursues them both far and near.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as birds dwelling in forest trees gather and disperse without constancy,
so it is with parents and kinsmen.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“If, moreover, there is a person who, in a place of tranquility, fixes their mindfulness in contemplation and cultivates wholesome karma, abandoning ignorance and darkness, as well as the violent and unrighteous acts of the fishing pole and the snare;
at the time of death, their body and mind will be free from affliction and devoid of all terror, and they will obtain rebirth in the heavens.

There, food and drink, clothing, and garments will be available according to their wishes; their retinue and palaces will all be perfectly complete; they will possess intelligence and wisdom, with no lack of necessities, gardens, or groves; and their lifespan and physical form will be fully perfected.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who deceives themselves and deludes the world—including their male and female relatives, friends, and acquaintances—by reviling, insulting, and humiliating them, thereby committing numerous unwholesome acts;
after the end of their life, they will fall into the various evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering.

Once they emerge from those states, if they are born among humans, they will be poor, lowly, and destitute of food and clothing; their male and female relatives will all feel weary of and seek to distance themselves from them.
Deluded and ignorant by false conceptions, they do not understand cause and effect; their minds are continuously associated with afflictions such as greed and hatred;
they have never cultivated virtuous deeds, and they constantly associate with evil friends and unrighteousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“In the hells one undergoes all manner of suffering, A burning born of one’s own karma;
In the human realm, one is entangled by suffering— All is created according to one’s own mind.”
"Within the three realms of saṃsāra, beings wander back and forth like ants circling a ring;
karma and its fruit act as mutual conditions, continuing in succession without end.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one attains the fruits of sainthood, one will finally escape saṃsāra; being free from all attachments, one dwells in sovereign peace and bliss, such that karma and its fruits can no longer cause one to waver."

Furthermore, if there are those who give rise to the delusions of greed and hatred and commit various misdeeds, they will fall into hell, where they are scorched by fierce flames; with their entire bodies undergoing all manner of suffering, they cry out in lamentation, yet though they contemplate means of escape, they cannot be liberated.
Such bitter and unpleasant karmic actions are created by the ignorant and deluded themselves;
they are like a fierce fire consuming a forest or wilderness, from which no grass or wood can escape.
Evil karma is likewise; one wanders through the hells, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions from which one cannot escape.

However, if there is a person who abandons evil friends, refrains from committing various wrongs, realizes the law of cause and effect, remains free from doubt and slander, cultivates right view, and takes faith and delight in True Suchness (Tathatā), they will attain tranquil peace and happiness, remaining far removed from saṃsāra and all suffering and affliction—this is supreme and beyond compare.

It is signless and unconditioned, free from delusion and inversion; it is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is sovereign and unimpeded, liberated from all fetters, and entirely remote from both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness, Volume One;
The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness, Volume Two.
Translated during the Great Song Dynasty by [the monk] from Magadha, Central India, Western Heaven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and State Preceptor Dharma-dāsa, a Śramaṇa conferred with the purple robe, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, the bhikṣus in the assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the burning of the hells and the immeasurable suffering endured therein, wept profusely with tears like rain. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they addressed him, saying:
“By what causal practices may these sentient beings undergoing punishment in these various hells avoid the painful afflictions of the future, escape their bondage, and swiftly attain liberation?”
"I only pray that, out of compassion and for the benefit of those in the future, you will expound upon this matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

Suppose there is a person who cultivates the various pure precepts, remaining free from false attachments, delusions, and perversions; who confesses all transgressions already committed so that they do not increase, and guards against those not yet committed so that they do not arise; who practices hearing, reflection, and various virtuous deeds; who abandons stinginess, greed, deceit, and violence; and who has deep faith in cause and effect.
"By virtue of these causes and conditions, one shall not undergo the suffering of the Burning Hell.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, if there is anyone who wishes to distance themselves from the enmity and harm of being burned, they should refrain from drinking various intoxicants and cultivate the practice of giving and the precepts."
Bhikṣus, you should know that the fault of alcohol is supreme; it destroys wholesome dharmas.
The fault of alcohol is supreme; it can ruin wisdom.
The fault of alcohol is supreme; it can ruin peace and happiness.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it distances one from virtuous friends.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it can give rise to all manner of diseases.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it destroys liberation.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme;
it provides an opportunity for enemies to prevail.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it causes one's wealth and possessions to be dissipated and destroyed.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it increases what is contrary to the Dharma.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it distances one from precious treasures.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it leads to the confused discourse of right and wrong.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it increases distraction.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it gives rise to greed and anger.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it causes ignorance to increase.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme: it turns loyalty into deceit;
the loss caused by alcohol is supreme: it reveals what was hidden;
the loss caused by alcohol is supreme: it causes afflictions to increase further.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it brings about rebirth in the hells.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it incinerates one's roots of goodness.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it destroys the Triple Gem.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it causes an evil reputation to spread.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it transforms intoxication into pus and blood.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it transforms fragrance into foul stench.
The loss caused by alcohol is supreme; it increases the three miserable realms.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that alcohol can destroy the karma of the form and formless realms;
alcohol can incinerate the noble karma of the four fruits."
Alcohol can increase violent and evil karma;
alcohol can lead one to disbelieve the true nature of cause and effect;
alcohol can increase the various sufferings of affliction.
Alcohol can give rise to the four verbal transgressions and matters of fear;
alcohol can repeatedly incite arrogance and deceit;
alcohol can cause one to slander virtuous friends and spiritual teachers.
Alcohol causes one to dwell perpetually in manifold sufferings and anxieties;
alcohol increases all manner of unwholesome states;
alcohol causes sentient beings to fall into the realm of darkness.
Alcohol causes sentient beings to fall among hungry ghosts and animals;
alcohol can distance one from intelligence and wisdom;
alcohol can distance one from the devas and immortals.
Alcohol can destroy the turning of the Wheel of the Dharma;
alcohol can increase and intensify lustful desire;
alcohol can ruin pure brahmacarya.
Alcohol increases pride and negligence;
alcohol is like the wind that destroys the world;
alcohol can ruin and disorder the conduct of an elder.
Alcohol can cause one to lose the mind of forbearance;
alcohol can delude the wisdom of those in the world;
alcohol can lead to the disparagement of the Dharma of liberation.
"Alcohol can cause one to distance oneself from the pure precepts of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Alcohol possesses such various faults and transgressions; it should be avoided."
Monks, you should know that those who drink alcohol crave only its delicious flavor and do not consider its bitter consequences.
With this as the cause, they fall into hell and undergo various sufferings;

when they emerge from hell and are reborn among humans, they are dull-witted and impoverished, they do not believe in cause and effect, they slander the True Dharma, they treat the virtuous with contempt, their afflictions increase, their lust blazes forth, they remain far removed from liberation, they are bound by violence and evil, they do not cultivate even a hair’s breadth of goodness, and they constantly associate with the causes of extreme wickedness.
Thus, transmigrating through the various realms of existence in this manner, there will be no time of liberation.

"Monks, you should know that by contemplating the departure from delusion and practicing right conduct, you must carefully guard the three karmas. Otherwise, one will receive the retribution of bitter and harsh sins—agonizing pain difficult to endure, certain to burn."
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should distance yourselves from all faults and transgressions, as well as from all fears.

Bhikṣus, you should know that what one does oneself, one must experience oneself; it cannot be avoided by others. The fruits of those ten unwholesome karmas, such as killing and so forth, are unfailingly realized.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Physical and verbal actions are not in vain; Through them, one wanders through the various evil realms.
Having bound oneself with what one has created, Even the Sugata cannot save one."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should distance oneself from all ill will and from false speech."
With this as the cause, one falls into the various evil realms and undergoes manifold sufferings;
later, when reborn among humans, one is impoverished and lowly, and whatever words one speaks mostly increase filth and evil, harming others like knives or axes;
it is also like hungry ghosts, who, summoned by their own karma, find that even food and drink burn them—this karma is likewise so.
It burns away all virtues, causing an evil reputation to spread, such that those who see or hear of it are displeased.

If there is a wise person who stays far from false speech and utters words that are truthful, everyone will believe and accept them; their beautiful name will spread abroad, just as when the fragrance of incense is smelled, all rejoice.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is another person who utters truthful speech—free from suffering, affliction, falsehood, and perverse attachments—it is like a precious jewel fit for use;
it is also like the light of a lamp that clearly illuminates forms and images.
True speech is likewise: all who hear it receive it with faith.”
By these causes and conditions, one attains sovereign liberation from all sufferings in the heavens.
Abandoning foul, evil, and false sounds, as well as mere calculation and worldly arts, one dwells in the most supreme state and proceeds toward liberation;

possessing immeasurable wealth, one universally relieves the poor and destitute; adorned with the light of wisdom, foremost among all, one’s treasuries are overflowing and one remains far removed from afflictions.

If born among humans, one will be most noble and eminent, fully endowed with various adornments and sovereign mastery; one will benefit sentient beings, bringing profit and happiness to all, from the solitary and the destitute to their spiritual friends.
One should always speak the truth; it is like fire or poison that burns and illuminates the most supreme and perilous paths, and like poison from which one must distance oneself.
Therefore, one should at all times abandon false speech, as well as all fetters, fears, and other such offenses.
"Furthermore, monks! Sentient beings who speak falsehoods fall into the Great Hell and undergo various sufferings, their bodies being torn asunder.
Just like blue lotuses, the executioners of Yama recite this verse for those offenders: [Verse follows]"
"The causes for the hell of falsehood are created by one's own mind amidst manifold sufferings;
though the waters of the Sāgara may come to an end, the retribution of this karma is inexhaustible."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, if there is a person who abandons false speech, it is as if they discard bitterness and astringency to obtain sweet and delicious flavor."

Bhikṣus, you should know that by cultivating wisdom and delighting in the truth, one adorns oneself with the most excellent merit; it is like nectar, capable of bringing one away from faults and calamities.

Fools, deluded and inverted, fail to understand the cause of suffering; they fervently create violent and evil karma, constantly and without ceasing committing every kind of harm, malice, and transgression. Consequently, they fall into the various hells, far removed from peace, happiness, and reality. Even if they obtain a human body, they find no joy in seeing or hearing [the Dharma];

their faults and afflictions increase, and they are loathed by dragons and devas. Deluded by falsehood, they treat virtuous friends as enemies; never having drawn near to them, they habitually practice all manner of evils, never abandoning them for even a moment. Thus they undergo the sufferings of saṃsāra without end.
Monks, you should know that this reality is supreme; when practiced by the wise, it is like ambrosia, free from faults and transgressions, and brings constant peace and happiness.
It is also like nirvana, where suffering and affliction do not intrude, and one is far removed from what is meaningless as well as the four marks and so forth.
Furthermore, just as the noble realm is the most supreme object of love and delight, so too is the truth; upon hearing it, all rejoice.
Again, just as a bright lamp is the most supreme thing in a dark room, for it can clearly reveal the forms of objects; so it is with the truth.
Reality is likewise: upon hearing it, one does not doubt or slander it.
Furthermore, just as a potent medicine can pacify suffering and affliction, and even cause malevolent spirits to depart, reality is likewise:
it brings liberation from the hells and all forms of suffering and affliction.

Deluded by ignorance within the various evil realms of saṃsāra, they undergo the inexhaustible karmic retributions of suffering as they pass from one state to another; falling into the various hells without finding liberation, they endure manifold sufferings while wailing and crying out.
A voice from the air addressed the sinners: "Do not weep;
you have created this for yourselves and must experience its results. Whom can you blame?
Your own minds are deluded and obscured by afflictions and false imaginings, such that you cannot distance yourselves from or liberate yourselves from these manifold sufferings."
Furthermore, if there is a person who constantly refrains from false speech, it is like ambrosia: all people love and delight in it, universally benefiting both themselves and others;
if one engages in false speech, it is like poison: it harms and afflicts both oneself and others, and no peace or security can be found.
Falsity is likewise; it causes one to fall into perilous places and undergo great suffering and affliction.
Such falsity should be abandoned throughout every lifetime, and one should cultivate pure conduct to be liberated from all sufferings.
The various wisdoms of true adornment suppress and sever all afflictions such as stinginess and greed, as well as unwholesome karma, leaving nothing remaining.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that sentient beings are deluded and bound by afflictions; they are like weapons, swords, and other such implements that harm sentient beings, preventing them from attaining peace and security."

Furthermore, if there is a person who truly abandons delusion and bestows the gifts of wealth and Dharma to benefit sentient beings, their most supreme merit shall be inexhaustible, leading even to the attainment of peace, happiness, and mastery.

“Furthermore, if there are those who distance themselves from reality and all forms of wisdom, constantly committing evil deeds and transmigrating through the various realms, they undergo manifold sufferings:

weapons and warfare, famine, wind, fire, and pestilence; being swept away, drowned, or burned; with enemies beyond count, a convergence of all manner of pains that oppress and cause agonizing distress.”
"All violent evils are self-inflicted and self-received; the retribution of karma is not in vain.

Bhikṣus, you should know that foolish people hold false attachments, recklessly asserting that this world and the next have no causes, no effects, and no functional efficacy. Through such distracted and arbitrary speculations, they increase what is unrighteous and distance themselves from wholesome dharmas."
Deluded sentient beings, failing to understand cause and effect, fall into the darkness and transmigrate without ceasing, their suffering and affliction being inexhaustible.
Out of great compassion, the Buddha has preached this rare Dharma to guide those who are deluded, causing their minds to achieve awakening and leading them to abandon all demons and terrors.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Sentient beings in the hells are dragged by their karma; dwelling in darkness, they constantly hear evil sounds and are bewildered by fear. They rush headlong into pits of fire that burn their bodies until their skin dries and their flesh rots like withered wood.
Yet, due to the power of karma, when a cool wind touches their bodies, they are restored to their original state and burned as before, undergoing immeasurable suffering."
"Experiencing suffering in this way, one is only released from it once the karma is exhausted.
Monks, you should know that by diligently cultivating wholesome karma, you will remain far removed from the evil realms and all forms of suffering and affliction."
May humans and devas enjoy wealth and happiness, possessing sovereignty and all that is lovely, and proceed toward nirvana;
may they subdue and eliminate greed, hatred, and all other afflictions so as not to be harmed by them;
may they abandon distraction and refrain from committing any evil deeds.
The hells are agonizing, where one constantly undergoes suffering; one should therefore give rise to weary detachment and seek liberation from saṃsāra.

Furthermore, if there are those who kill sentient beings, take what is not given, slander the Triple Gem, do not believe in cause and effect, and engage in deceitful and divisive actions of body and so forth;
or if they are characterized by stinginess, greed, and jealousy, never relinquishing them—[they shall fall into the hells].
After the end of their lives, they fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering;
thus they transmigrate and sink into the evil realms, never attaining liberation.
"Monks, you should know that by the power of past karma, one revolves through birth and death, bound within the various states of existence without end."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"With unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind as their cause, one falls into hell and undergoes suffering throughout the three periods of time, without even a moment's respite."
It would be better to take up a sharp blade and sever the root of the tongue than to use this tongue to speak of matters of defiled desire. Why is this?
Because with this as a cause, one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, extensively creating evil karma, wandering through the various realms of existence without attaining liberation.

All this is due to delusion and false imaginings; by perversely clinging to defiled desire, one perceives suffering as pleasure, giving rise to karmic afflictions that cannot be escaped throughout the long duration of birth and death.
Furthermore, just as a lasso entangles and binds sentient beings, so too does defiled desire bind them, causing them to fall into hell and reap bitter fruits of suffering.

Deluded sentient beings are unable to distance themselves from the causes and conditions of defiled desire; their flattery, deception, and violence increase and blaze ever more fiercely, incinerating all manner of wholesome virtues, while lacking compassion and failing to bring broad benefit to sentient beings.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that the grasping at a self is like a mountain; evil karma is like the ocean; and the flames of affliction are fiercely blazing and continuous, entangling one without release. Its appearance is hideous, and it brings alarm, fear, and distress, never being peaceful or secure.”

Furthermore, just as space pervades all places, so too do afflictions, karma, and suffering constantly follow sentient beings, never abandoning them and being present everywhere; they bind sentient beings, preventing their escape.

Furthermore, just as in the world those with false views cling to a self, which is so firm it is difficult to uproot; bound by their perverse attachments, they never momentarily let go. Oppressed by suffering and tormented by violence, they endure harm and hardship, without protection or refuge. They revolve through birth and death, pervading all realms like a blazing fire, undergoing various sufferings without end.

"Furthermore, this grasping at a self is inverted, false, ignorant, and delusive; one may grasp at the stars, or reckon with the five faculties, or grasp at the mental faculty, falsely taking them to be ultimate and relying upon or serving them in the hope of attaining liberation."
Due to false attachment, they conceive, "I am the one who creates causes and the one who experiences results.

Consequently, they increase the suffering and affliction of body and mind, rather than distancing themselves from the bitter pains of the cycle of hellish rebirths. With stubborn persistence and fierce intensity, they remain entangled in a continuous stream, deludedly committing various unwholesome karmas;
they do not feel remorse, nor do they contemplate skillful means to awaken to the nature of cause and effect, abandon faults and transgressions, and strive for liberation.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if there are those who commit various evil deeds, they will undergo the retribution of hardship, remaining in hell until the kalpa is destroyed, yet still not attaining liberation;
neither the nāgas nor the devas of the eight classes can protect them.”
Why is this so? These sentient beings are dragged by the ropes of their own karma and undergo the sufferings of hell.
Once this world-system has been destroyed, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, they go to other regions elsewhere to undergo suffering, unable to escape it.
"If there is another person who conceives the intent to kill their own parents and acts upon this resolve, this offense is most grave!
For example, even if someone were to destroy all sentient beings within the three realms with a sharp sword, it would still be lighter than this."
Why is this? To harbor resentment and inflict harm upon one's own parents for their kindness and virtue is a transgression of extreme gravity.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who causes a schism in the Sangha’s harmony, kills an Arhat, or sheds the blood of a Buddha, these offenses are the most serious of all!
Receiving retribution without interval, they undergo continuous suffering; beset by violence and dread, they are subjected to punishment at all times.
Contemplating [the means of escape], they find no moment’s rest;
iron, poison, and flaming torches inflict endless torment. Bound by unrighteousness, they face destruction and terror, which persists eternally without interruption.

Deluded by perversion and ignorance, they are unable to distance themselves from the bitter fruits [of their actions]; due to these causes and conditions, they are dragged along by afflictions and karma, transmigrating through birth and death without attaining liberation.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that you must cultivate revulsion toward sensual desire and false speech; through reflection on regret, you should subdue and eliminate them, renounce them, and bring to rest all craving and attachment.”
Do not entertain such thoughts, much less cling to them or create karma based upon them.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should destroy the turbulence of the afflictions and the perversity of wrong views.
Within the various evil realms, one abandons those karmas, delusions, and so forth, and strives for the unsurpassed, most excellent, and boundless wisdom of the two emptinesses.

One benefits sentient beings so that they do not fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, where they would be incinerated by various sufferings and undergo manifold undesirable fruits.
“If there are further persons who revere the Buddha, the Sangha, and all the scriptures, honoring and making offerings to them, singing praises and extolling their virtues;

by these causes and conditions, they will distance themselves from defilements, dust, and all fetters, as well as karmic obstacles. They shall obtain the reward of peace and happiness, always being reborn in the auspicious realms, characterized by goodness in the beginning, middle, and end, remaining far removed from suffering and affliction, with this state of peace and happiness continuing for a long time without interruption.”

Abandoning defilements and all afflictions, subduing and eliminating ignorance, delusion, intoxication, and agitation so that they do not arise; bringing rest to saṃsāra and liberating oneself from all states of existence, until finally one realizes the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Thereupon the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If there is another person who, through deceitful and false speech, deludes the world, seeking wealth and profit to sustain their own life and that of their slaves, horses, and so forth."

Due to these causes and conditions, after their lives end, they will inevitably fall into hell to undergo the suffering of being burned; fierce flames will blaze forth continuously without interruption, and they will be scorched and boiled in agony without end.
That they undergo such violent and evil suffering is entirely due to the牵引 (karmic attraction) of their own actions; they cannot escape the various sufferings of hell.
It is like a lasso that binds sentient beings, rendering them powerless;

this karma is likewise able to bind sentient beings and cause them to fall into fierce flames that burn their bodies, hands, feet, bones, and marrow, all of which become like masses of fire, both internally and externally, resulting in immeasurable anguish.
That great hell has four gates on its perimeter and four corners, each of which is ablaze;
with pus, blood, and excrement, and various forms of punishment, many instruments of suffering all emit smoke and flames, burning simultaneously in a continuous, uninterrupted succession.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Deluded sentient beings, Greedy for wealth, practice deception;
Dragged by the karma of hell, They are consumed by fire and undergo all manner of suffering."
Just as various poisons, when drunk by oneself, bring harm back upon oneself;
so too it is with the karma one creates—it follows one constantly like a shadow.
Furthermore, it is like the fire-drill wood: the fire produced from it can consume the wood itself.
"Suffering follows from evil causes; what one has done oneself, one must experience oneself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone who gives rise to craving toward an object, they should practice a contemplation that can serve as an antidote."
If one gives rise to craving for precious jewels, one should contemplate them as being like a whirling firebrand or as something subject to destruction.
Since worldly craving and attachment are immeasurable and boundless, through such contemplation, they are all entirely abandoned.
One should regard attachment to the world as one would an enemy;
seeing the waters of the ocean, one should conceive the thought of being swept away and drowned;
seeing swords and blades, one should conceive the thought of extinguishing afflictions.
When rain falls from the clouds, one should form the thought of universal benefit;
when seeing the Buddhas, one should form the thought of liberation;
when seeing a king, one should give rise to the thought of reverence.
When seeing one's parents, one should conceive the thought of affection;
when conceiving stinginess and greed, one should regard them as poisonous medicine;
when seeing one's kinsmen, one should conceive the thought of temporary rest.
When approaching parinirvāṇa, one should give rise to the perception of equanimity;
when maintaining pure precepts, one should give rise to the perception of radiance;
and when seeing gold and jewels, one should give rise to the perception of their fragility and destruction.
Seeing those who violate the precepts, one should conceive the thought of rescuing and protecting them;
when wealth is lost or scattered, one should conceive the thought that it is not ultimate;
and while dwelling within the triple world, one should conceive the thought that it is like a prison.
When seeing the solar disk, one should give rise to the perception of wisdom;
when practicing meditative concentration, one should seek the perception of merit.
"Monks, you should know that to feign various practices regarding the wealth and property of others and to steal it through deception and falsehood—this is [unwholesome]."
With this as the cause, they fall into the hells, where various agonies incinerate their bodies and their limbs are torn asunder; they dwell perpetually in darkness without any light.
Delusion obscures their minds, which they never abandon; they lack even the slightest peace and remain far removed from nirvana.

When one lifetime’s retribution is exhausted, they fall again among ghosts and animals, constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, exhaustion from forced labor, and a myriad of sufferings that are without end.

If born among humans, they will lack wealth and resources; their desire for sensual pleasure will be intense, and they will dwell in a lowly and base station, enduring continuous toil and hardship without even a moment's rest.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Deceiving others and stealing their wealth, one shall personally undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms;
hunger and thirst will perpetually continue, and all manner of pains will never cease."
"Delusion obscures wisdom, and light is perpetually absent;
wandering through the miserable realms of saṃsāra, one can only emerge when karma is exhausted.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who gives rise to defiled attachment toward objects of pleasant and agreeable touch, and does not constantly abandon them, they should cultivate the perception of these as being hard, bitter, and harsh;

as impermanent and subject to decay, their essence is not ultimate, like lightning or a dream, and their intrinsic nature is non-existent. Thus, they should remain entirely detached from all such pleasant touches."
A bhikṣu should know that he must not give rise to attachment toward the objects of desire;
furthermore, he should renounce all lovely and defiling sensory objects belonging to the world, whether past or future.
