At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Furthermore, if there are those in future ages who seek rebirth among humans or devas and wish to become weary of and detached from the fruits of suffering, they should distance themselves from all karmic afflictions, violence, lust, dissipation, and false speech; they should cease harming or distressing any sentient being, cultivate various wholesome deeds, and cause them to gradually increase and continue at all times, thereby obtaining the retribution of peace and happiness and abandoning all suffering and distress."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who can distance themselves from violence and cruelty will not encounter bitter fruits;
Free from slander and false speech, all who hear their name will rejoice."
"Subdue and eliminate the thieves of past enmity and false attachments so that they do not arise again;
awaken to the defilements of affliction and constantly cultivate all their remedies.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Furthermore, if anyone encounters adverse conditions, they should awaken to themselves and others;

they should destroy and distance themselves from false conceptual attachments, contemplate the noble sages, and cultivate the practice of patience. Moreover, regarding wealth and possessions, they should abandon greedy delusions;

toward humans and non-humans, worldly and world-transcending realms, the right path and the wrong path, men and women, the fruits of good and evil karma, the real and the unreal, palaces and dwellings, respectful offerings, and even all objects of defilement and purity, they should not give rise to false attachments, nor should they harbor hatred or envy."

Truly departing from delusion, one feels compassion for sentient beings, enters the gradual stages of the noble ones, distances oneself from hell, destroys Yama, eliminates darkness, and cultivates wisdom.
Greed and anger are the causes of defilement, like fire or poison; one should abandon them entirely.
Since the retribution of karma is arduous, one should confess and reveal one's transgressions, rather than concealing them.
"Having clearly understood these words, one should proclaim the cause of suffering and ensure that all remain far removed from it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, if there is anyone who encounters evil friends or the retinues of others, they should not give rise to hatred or envy, but should instead form this thought:"

"Since beginningless time, throughout many kalpas, I have transmigrated through the various realms of existence; my parents, kinsmen, and virtuous friends and teachers have likewise wandered through birth and death, coming and going without fixed destination.
Toward all sentient beings, I ought to give rise to compassion and thoughts of affection."
"By this, afflictions such as greed and hatred are distanced.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"If there is another person who, through false and divisive speech, creates estrangement between this party and that, what fruit will they experience?"
“We pray that the Buddha will expound this for us; we long to hear it so as to benefit all sentient beings of the future.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“You should know that there are briefly ten kinds of retributions obtained for divisive speech.”
What are the ten? First, one's lineage is lowly and base, and one's kinsmen are estranged;
second, one is distanced from virtuous friends while evil companions increase in number.
Third, being foolish, dull-witted, and increasing one's transgressions and faults;
fourth, slandering the noble and holy ones while disbelieving in cause and effect;
fifth, concealing and protecting one’s own failings while delighting in speaking of the faults of others.
Sixth, falsehoods increase while acts of loyalty and integrity become scarce;
seventh, one falls into hell after death, suffering endless torment;
eighth, one gives rein to greed and anger, causing an evil reputation to spread.
Ninth, wealth and goods shall be lost, leading to constant sorrow and suffering;
tenth, one shall be separated from the True Dharma and constantly born in remote borderlands.
Monks, you should know that such is the retribution for the karma of divisive speech; you must not cling to it, but rather abandon it entirely.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who utter coarse and evil speech, what kind of fruit do they experience?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"One should know that there are ten retributions obtained for verbal karma. What are these ten?
First, the mouth emits flames like blades that burn one's own body;"
Second, their false views are rampant, such that there is no evil they will not commit;
third, they distance themselves from sages and worthies while daily increasing their circle of evil friends;
fourth, the multitude all detest and abandon them as if they were various poisons.
Fifth, the external environment is treacherous and narrow, with uneven elevations;
sixth, afflictions blaze fiercely, destroying and scattering wealth and goods;
seventh, they incinerate all roots of goodness, while unrighteousness increases ever further.
Eighth, their bodies become foul-smelling and filthy, such that all who smell them feel revulsion;
ninth, their limbs and joints wither and dry up, and they suffer from constant illness;
tenth, they die and fall into perilous realms, transmigrating through the cycle of birth and death.
“Monks, you should know that such is the retribution brought about by the karmic action of harsh speech; you should keep yourselves far away from it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“All wholesome deeds should be cherished, Like a father and like a mother.”
The beautiful and good bring peace and stability, enabling one to remain free from clamor and strife;
the beautiful and good are a joy to humans and devas; the beautiful and good increase diligence and valor;
the beautiful and good bring many kinsmen and followers; the beautiful and good lead to liberation from the three miserable realms.
"Excellence stills all evils; excellence leaves behind afflictions.
One who can cast off verbal transgressions should cultivate all manner of virtues.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Such harsh and abusive speech as has been uttered must be entirely abandoned; it should be subdued and eliminated so that it does not arise again or increase, lest one fall into hell and undergo the sufferings of hunger and thirst, along with various pains and afflictions."

In those evil realms, they are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst as if consumed by fire; they perpetually long for food and drink, yet cannot obtain even as much as a mustard seed, let alone a full meal!
“Bhikṣus, you should know that those sentient beings, bound by this evil karma and its extreme suffering, are incessantly oppressed by the flames of hunger and thirst, with not a moment’s respite.”
Such bitter fruits as these are all summoned and experienced due to false and coarse verbal karma.
Monks, you should know that false and evil karma, as well as all merits and the superior virtues of humans and devas, are all created by the mind.

If delusion predominates, one will despise the virtuous and good, give rise to unwholesome mental karma, and distance oneself from equanimity. Delighting in speaking of the long and short, the right and wrong of others—just as a lamp’s light gradually dims when the oil is nearly exhausted—one’s wisdom diminishes and transgressions increase.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should always remain far removed from false and evil karma so that it does not cause you harm;
as for the fame and profit of others, if you give rise to envy, anger, or other such states, they will afflict and disturb your body and mind without a moment’s respite.

Monks, you should know that these evil causes incinerate one's own merit; in future lives, they will inevitably bring about the fruits of suffering and cause one to wander in saṃsāra without rest. You should therefore abandon them.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who constantly give rise to anger and resentment toward both animate and inanimate things, what retribution will they receive?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“You should know that anger and resentment will result in ten kinds of decline in future lives. What are these ten?”
First, enemies will increase in number, and all people will feel aversion toward them;
second, they will be born in borderlands, far removed from the True Dharma;
third, they will be entangled by various illnesses and suffer from poverty and hardship.
Fourth, after death they fall among jackals and wolves, in treacherous and violent circumstances;
fifth, they may dwell among venomous snakes, constantly full of anger and resentment;
sixth, their faculties are ugly and deformed, and they are estranged from their kin.
Seventh, they die and fall into the Black Rope Hell, where their suffering continues without interruption;
eighth, their limbs wither and dry up, as they are scorched by manifold sufferings;
ninth, their false attachments increase, and they slander the noble sages.
Tenth, they dwell perpetually within the three miserable realms, revolving without respite.
These ten types [of suffering] all arise from anger and hatred.
Monks, you should know that you must distance yourselves from them all.
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who constantly cultivate non-anger, what retribution do they obtain?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"One attains ten benefits. What are these ten?
First, one's excellence becomes widely known;..."
Second, they remain far removed from pride and arrogance;
third, they are able to subdue anger and hatred;
fourth, they abandon the three miserable realms.
Fifth, enemies shall not invade;
sixth, one shall always be reborn among humans or devas;
seventh, one’s retinue shall be complete.
Eighth, his faculties are unimpaired;
ninth, he is endowed with perfect physical marks;
tenth, he has achieved liberation.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that such are the benefits; you must cultivate them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Deterioration arises from the karma of anger, Sinking into the depths of the ocean of suffering.”
The various faculties are mostly deficient and deformed; oppressed by hardships, they cannot endure their burdens.

Through virtuous causes one is born in the happy realms, while through unrighteousness one enters the Avīci hell, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts; good and evil karma follow one constantly.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The karmas of good and evil differ in their capacity for harm or benefit; they increase and decrease in relation to one another. According to the power of karma, the retribution received is never in vain."
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If sentient beings are stingy and greedy, failing to practice generosity; being without reliance, deluded, ignorant, and foolish; lacking faith in cause and effect, and slandering the noble and holy ones—what kind of retribution will they receive?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there are sentient beings who are stingy, greedy, and lacking faith;
who do not even enjoy various material goods themselves, let alone give them to others."
"Monks, you should know that ignorant fools,
having distanced themselves from virtuous friends and further committing various misdeeds,
will by reason of these causes and conditions fall into the various hells and suffer without end."
When those bhikṣus heard these words, they were filled with sorrow and distress; their voices choked with grief, they wept aloud.
They further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At what time shall these sentient beings finally cast off this suffering?"
"I pray that the Buddha will expound this for the benefit of future generations.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus and spoke in verse:
"Sixty thousand human years constitute one day and night for Apadā."
Accumulating those years and months, totaling thirty-six thousand;
by virtue of this remaining lifespan, it increases by twenty thousand in each subsequent stage.
In the eight cold great hells, suffering continues without end.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The sentient beings who suffer in this great hell did so because, through their body, speech, and mind, they treated the virtuous with contempt, slandered the True Dharma, committed unrighteous acts, destroyed Buddha images, burned the scriptures, reviled the authentic Dharma, and spoke words devoid of meaning.”
"Due to this karmic cause, sentient beings are drawn into perilous and evil places, where they undergo various punishments and suffer continuously without end.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is another person who reads, recites, and expounds the profound sūtras of the Buddha’s true Dharma, causing others to believe and accept them and to resolve upon bodhicitta, what kind of supreme benefit will they obtain?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The merit is immeasurable, subtle, and most supreme!

These sentient beings, who receive, uphold, read, and recite such a profound Dharma, who expound and explain it, who practice in accordance with the Dharma, and who give rise to right faith; [their merit is immeasurable]."

Prostrate and eliminate obstructive defilements, remaining far removed from the evil realms; always dwelling among humans and devas in peace, security, and happiness; protected, assisted, and praised by all noble sages.
In future lives, one shall attain the supreme: extensive learning, dhāraṇī-retention, merit, and wisdom;
as well as mindfulness and non-forgetfulness.
Palaces and precious jewels shall all be fully provided;
they shall swiftly achieve the realization of parinirvāṇa;
and they shall forever be free from old age and illness, from stinginess, greed, envy, jealousy, delusion, intoxication, confusion, slander of the True Dharma, falsehood, and perverse attachments.
"One will be able to remain far removed from the eight difficulties and hardships, as well as all that is contrary to the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Furthermore, if there are those who are deluded and errant in their attachments, who take delight in the false and illusory things of the world, and extensively commit various unwholesome acts;"

Regarding what they have done, they feel no regret; their minds become increasingly intense as various evils continue in succession. They do not fear dangerous places and distance themselves from virtuous friends.
Due to these karmic causes, they will revolve through the hells and experience bitter fruits of suffering; this is certainly not false.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that all those who possess wisdom completely abandon all unwholesome karmas and, having engendered right faith, cultivate their antidotes.
Bhikṣus, you should know that one creates offenses through the mind and likewise reaps their fruits;
that one is liberated from birth and death and wanders through the various realms of existence is also due to the mind.”

One can practice flattery and deception, yet also achieve self-mastery; one can be violent and cruel, and thus fall into the three miserable realms, obtaining great terror—all this arises from the mind.
Furthermore, one can renounce [unwholesome states] and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, yet also turn one's back upon true peace and happiness.
Furthermore, one is able to remain far removed from falsehoods and inversions, as well as the various distinctions among causes, conditions, and karmic retributions;

whether provisional or real, whether the resulting retribution is certain or uncertain, beneficial or not beneficial, and whether wholesome or unwholesome—one is able to distance oneself from all such things.
It can also manifest the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; just as a bright lamp can dispel darkness and further reveal various forms and images, so too is the mind.
Furthermore, just as good and evil, with their distinct causes and effects, follow one another and never depart, such that one wanders through the various realms of existence due to the mind;

and just as defilement and purity, concealment and manifestation, though different, mutually increase and decrease, so too the provisional and the real, and principle and phenomena, are neither identical nor separate.

Right view and false attachment, karma of the desirable and undesirable, liberation and saṃsāra—these principles are neither identical to nor separate from one another, yet all are created by the mind.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the bonds of various karmas cause beings to wander through birth and death like a snare; they bind sentient beings, such that they are never independent."

Deluded by ignorance and false conceptions, bound by afflictions, and shrouded by obstructions, they prevent wisdom from arising; thus, they cannot discern between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
Furthermore, this is not the practice for attaining realization, and the truth of the two-fold emptiness has no means of being manifested or realized.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that this arises from ignorance, which deludes one regarding the correct principle; it has never led to any realization of the Buddha’s teachings, but rather creates obstacles and hindrances.
Not practicing oneself, one further obstructs the learning of others, falsely accusing them of errors and faults, thereby deeply increasing their weariness and detachment.”

Due to these karmic causes, having slandered the True Dharma and acted as enemies and thieves to the Buddhas, they are deluded and ignorant from lifetime to lifetime, constantly falling into the dark hells where they undergo all manner of sufferings without end.

Having emerged from there, they fall further into the realm of hungry ghosts; foolish, confused, violent, and evil, they harm one another, constantly suffering under the oppression of hunger and thirst without a moment’s rest, enduring various kinds of pain.

Emerging from that state again, they fall among the animals, exhausted, famished, and bound by manifold sufferings that never cease; their anger increases with ferocity as they devour one another, their extremely wicked dispositions continuing without interruption.
"Just as the fire of the world can burn forests and wilds, so too does this karma; it can incinerate all virtues and bring harm to sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Deluded sentient beings, Slandering the Buddha and destroying the True Dharma..."
Falling into the three miserable realms, one cannot emerge even after the exhaustion of kalpas;
dwelling eternally in the suffering of hell, shrouded in darkness with no light,
as hungry ghosts and animals, hunger and thirst are without end.
"Sentient beings, bound by karma, Enshrouded by wisdom-defiling afflictions,
Sunk in the perilous and evil ocean, Cannot escape even when the kalpa is destroyed.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Due to the causal karma of slandering the Dharma mentioned previously, they will transmigrate through the three miserable realms and undergo immeasurable suffering. Once they emerge from those states, if they are born among humans, they will be impoverished and distressed, with deficient sense faculties, oppressed by hunger and thirst, and their afflictions will increase. Their nature will be violent and evil, like that of an elephant or a horse—stubborn and untamable—and they will be constantly associated with folly, delusion, and false attachments.

They will be bound by the suffering of illness without interruption; their minds will be dissolute, grasping at false objects of perception without ceasing for a moment; and they may be deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired. Failing to encounter the True Dharma, they will always dwell in borderlands, lacking wisdom and possessed of foolishness and false attachments, undergoing various sufferings without end."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that the retribution for the sin of slandering the Dharma is immeasurable; it cannot be fully described.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Furthermore, if there is someone who cultivates the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and strives for liberation, who does not give rise to slander against the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, but always honors, praises, and faithfully accepts them—regarding them as parents and as virtuous friends, constantly protecting, respecting, and faithfully accepting them, never giving rise to false slander, and causing their hearts to rejoice.”
Then, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should sentient beings abandon faults and non-virtues and cultivate sublime practices?
We pray that the Buddha will expound this for the benefit of future generations.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen closely, listen closely!
I shall now speak for you.”
Furthermore, if there is a person who abandons all unwholesome actions of body and speech and constantly cultivates wholesome deeds;
who dwells in and observes the three periods of time, subdues all false pride, honors the Triple Gem, exerts diligence in the three types of action to realize bodhi;
and who, throughout the three times, remains free from all attachments as well as greed, hatred, and the like.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

By remaining free from all faults and afflictions regarding the three types of action, you abide in the joyful practice of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*). You proceed toward the three types of awakening and the three suchnesses (*tri-tathatā*), distancing yourself from afflictions and abiding in contemplation, thereby equalizing the mind and observing the most excellent;
furthermore, being free from pride and doubt, your three actions are purified, subduing and eliminating obstructive defilements."

In all places, one is able to sever all bonds and cultivate right practice; recollecting suffering and emptiness, one inclines toward liberation. Subtle and profound, one distances oneself from all evils and initiates skillful means to destroy ignorance and all forms of craving.

Therefore, bhikṣus! You should cultivate wholesome conduct and abandon all that is unwholesome. You should be able to distance yourselves from hunger and thirst, cold and heat, emaciated countenances, the ravages of ignorance and darkness, and the sorrows, afflictions, and regrets; you should completely relinquish all such various sufferings.

You should attain the wealth, abundance, peace, and happiness of humans and devas, possess wisdom and extensive learning, and constantly practice the cultivation of equanimity, as well as making offerings of incense, lamps, flower garlands, necklaces, and other articles of worship.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

If one gives rise to false attachments, stinginess, greed, jealousy, falsehood, flattery, and deception, one will fall among the hungry ghosts (preta) and undergo various sufferings and afflictions—oppressed and harmed in an uninterrupted succession, scorched by hunger and thirst."
"When the causes of karma ripen, not even a hair's breadth can be avoided;
bound by sorrow and suffering, one remains far removed from liberation.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How may these sentient beings be liberated from such manifold sufferings?
At what time shall they attain liberation and acquire right faith?
As I contemplate this now, I am unable to fully comprehend it."

Furthermore, these sentient beings within the realm of hungry ghosts endure hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the suffering of grief for long periods, day and night; their bodies and heads wither away, and they remain perpetually shrouded by the darkness of delusion, without even a moment’s respite.
"I pray that the Buddha will expound this teaching for the benefit of future generations.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"These sentient beings, in past lives, committed various evil deeds; they did not cultivate merit or wisdom, but were stingy, jealous, and deceitful. Their afflictions were fiercely blazing, and they gave rein to greed and anger, unable to subdue or eliminate them."
After their lives end, they fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering;

having emerged from there, they again fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), oppressed by manifold sufferings and bound by hunger and thirst. In every place and at all times they experience suffering, without rescue or refuge. Longing for food and drink, they ultimately find nothing; wailing in regret and lamentation, they think: "When shall I ever be rid of this suffering?"

“Bhikṣus, you should know that ignorant sentient beings, bound by the afflictions, revolve through the three miserable realms due to the three types of unwholesome karma and undergo such suffering as this.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know that if there are laymen or laywomen, or gods, Māras, or Brahmās,

who destroy their evil karma and cultivate wholesome dharmas, who delight in the True Dharma and carefully contemplate the four great elements and the five aggregates of their own bodies as suffering,
empty, and impermanent; and who further perceive them as being like water bubbles, plantain trunks, dreams, or lightning— all of which are entirely illusory.”
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should cultivate and increase all wholesome dharmas;
regarding all evils, apply their antidotes so that they do not arise;
and you shall dwell securely among humans and devas, attaining mastery over all that is most excellent and desirable.
Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, one remains far removed from all that is improper;

having resolutely abandoned falsehood, deception, and all forms of fear, one takes delight in the supreme, engages in tranquil reflection, and, free from all distraction, performs manifold virtues. From beginning to middle to end, these are maintained without interruption; the sense faculties are subdued, and one relinquishes all bonds and the miserable realms.

"Shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, they do not understand cause and effect; they extensively commit unwholesome deeds and transmigrate through the three miserable realms, undergoing manifold sufferings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one delights in dwelling [in this world], One should contemplate the suffering of the womb."
Far removed from inverted craving, destroy it so that it does not arise;
bound by the ropes of karma, the sufferings of the three realms are endless.
Coming and going like ants in a circle, one sinks and is difficult to escape.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death entwine sentient beings, never leaving them."
It is just like fish or deer caught in nets or ensnared by arrows;
it is exactly so. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Craving is like poison, and anger is like fire. Falsehood, flattery, and deception delude and obscure the pure mind. Blazing afflictions constantly pursue one another, preventing one from attaining liberation."

Furthermore, if there are those who greedily seek wealth and property, extensively practicing deception to sustain their lives, they are bound by false attachments and revolve through the various realms of existence.
This is like a fish swallowing a hook, arising from greed;
it is like water in a mirage, born of the mind of craving.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Deluded attachment to false views, Through karmic conditions, there is an illusory body.
When cause and fruit are forever free from inversion, That which is apart from cause and fruit is not the truth."
The cause of saṃsāra is affliction; by thoroughly realizing and attaining true emptiness, one is liberated and free from afflictions. The principle of reality is not non-existent.
In the state of supreme, wondrous enlightenment, both obstacles are entirely extinguished.
"Tranquil and eternally unmoving, Bringing benefit and joy to all sentient beings.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there should be another person who gives rise to slander and lack of faith, destroying the Three Jewels, and making a living by trading flowers, fruits, and other goods."
Due to these causes and conditions, they fall into the evil destinies;

there, wild foxes and various vultures with beaks as sharp as vajras, possessing hideous forms, harass and terrify them, gathering to devour their flesh, hands, feet, eyes, and marrow until nothing remains, as they undergo immeasurable suffering.

Bound by the cords of karma, pursued and never abandoned, they have no one to rely upon and receive no rescue. Thus they revolve, wandering back and forth through the three evil realms without ever ceasing;

having emerged from those states, they fall again among the hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, their manifold sufferings increasing as they vomit flames from their mouths, which continue like a mountain range without interruption.
"Even if a great rain were to fall everywhere, this fire of evil karma could never be extinguished.
Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is anyone who cultivates generosity, ethical discipline, and even wisdom, they will be able to liberate themselves from all manner of sufferings."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

Taking evil karma as their cause, beings invite the fruits of the three miserable realms; deluded and attached, they are unable to subdue and eliminate the one hundred and twenty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of both discriminative and innate afflictions."

Within the three realms, there are twelve modes of practice regarding the four truths of the desire realm; when combined with the two higher realms, there are twenty-four modes of practice as explained in relation to the three realms.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
There are sixteen aspects of the Four Truths and the Four Knowledges, as well as the two paths of vision;

one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the eight factors of the noble path, the five faculties, and the five powers, thereby liberating oneself from violence and evil, and remaining far removed from the conflagration."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus! One should cultivate the two supreme truths with wisdom, as well as the three foundations of mindfulness;
thus one remains far removed from all Māras and hungry ghosts, and from the sufferings of hunger and thirst, while increasing the wholesome dharmas (śukladharma)."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The ten evils are created by the mind; The path of sinking and wandering is perilous.
Bound by the objects of greed and delusion, The resulting retribution will surely follow."
The realms of hell are extreme suffering; alas, there is no refuge!
Conditions ripen like shadows and echoes; when the kalpa of destruction comes, retribution is difficult to avoid.
Diligently apply oneself to the three karmas, cultivate extensive learning, and practice dhāraṇī.
Cultivating the two adornments through the six perfections, One fully realizes bodhi.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Furthermore, if there is a person who cultivates the three wholesome karmas:”

Through generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning, one abandons violence, evil, delusion, and craving, thereby attaining liberation from all suffering and escaping the unwholesome realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts.
Bhikṣus, you should know that those in the realms of hungry ghosts undergo various sufferings:
cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and the oppression of painful afflictions from which they cannot escape.
Due to these evil karmas—namely, arrogance and deceit—they have fallen into the three miserable paths.
Within that realm of rebirth, they harm one another, perpetually bound by greed and hatred without ever letting go.

Due to having previously abandoned generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning, they have committed various misdeeds; they cannot discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and being utterly deluded regarding right faith, they fail to achieve awakening.
"Because of these obstacles, one cannot cultivate the wholesome realms of humans and devas, nor can one examine matters such as gain and loss.
Then, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what karma is the realm of the asuras brought about?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively; I shall now speak for you.
That asura, due to his past deceit and falsehood, and being constantly bound and unable to abandon the karma of crookedness and various afflictions, fell into that realm."
Furthermore, due to lack of faith, they slander the virtuous and good; failing to comprehend the true nature of cause and effect, they fall into those miserable realms and lack wisdom.
Deluded and clinging to false attachments, they are filled with fear and dread, never finding peace or security.
At that time, Śakra and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. They then addressed the Buddha in verse:
"The level path of the three vehicles, Proclaimed by the Muni himself;
The principle of true emptiness and outflowlessness, Its fundamental essence free from all entanglements."
"Arising compassion extensively in response to sentient beings, Holding deep pity for those in suffering,
His radiance shines eternally, Never abandoning the mind that benefits others.
At that time, having spoken this verse, Śakra joined his palms in reverence and stood to one side.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"You should cultivate the pure Dharma of the Three Vehicles, which is free from all fetters, equal, and pure;
it can leave behind narrow and perilous paths, sever all darkness, and is luminous and untainted."
Like a precious jewel, its essential nature is pure; the devas rejoice, delighting in this most supreme state, practicing it with tranquility and upholding it without forsaking it.
Furthermore, they observe and take delight in ethical discipline, generosity, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Just as the various devas respectfully serve their celestial lords, remaining free from transgressions and looking up to them with veneration;
so too do they treat all sentient beings with gentleness and harmony.

If one is born in the heavens, one attains a pure and wondrous body, remaining far removed from greed and anger; one extinguishes dust and defilements as well as all sensory objects, and through the causes and conditions of greed and resentment, one is liberated from drowning. One destroys all states of existence (*bhava*) and becomes entirely free from the mutual hatred and jealousy among kinsmen and associates, as well as the mud of the five desires.
Dwelling among all sentient beings, they remain ever-humble, respectful, and harmonious.
They abide in constant goodness, skillfully distancing themselves from all defilements; their deportment is orderly and disciplined as they shake off afflictions and subdue Māra.
Abiding in wisdom, supremely pure, they well protect the three karmas and constantly practice meditative concentration.
Abandoning evil friends and non-celibate conduct, they are forever free from fetters and always dwell among the devas.
"Virtuous friends and spiritual mentors encourage and inspire the Great Mind, so that one may swiftly ascend to the other shore.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly; they delighted in hearing the profound Dharma and gazed upon him with leaping joy.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"If there are those who love and delight in the devas, experiencing superior and wondrous bliss, and do not fall into the three miserable realms, by practicing what causes and actions do they obtain such excellent retribution?"
"We pray that the Buddha will expound this for the benefit of future generations.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is anyone who constantly practices giving, maintains the precepts, and cultivates meditative concentration; whose resolve is firm, who increases their cultivation, who remains far removed from bonds, defiled desires, and various entanglements; who does not give rise to transgressions, who causes wisdom to increase and become luminous, and who extensively cultivates all manner of goodness."
After the end of their lives, they will be born by transformation among the devas, possessing sovereign and unimpeded power, with perfect physical forms and incomparable wealth and joy.

They will have many kinsmen, virtuous friends, and spiritual mentors who live in mutual harmony and accord; they will be humble and respectful, free from pride, and will delight in the profound Dharma.
Constantly encountering the preaching and exhortations of sages and worthies, they distance themselves from the three poisons and all unwholesome karmas.
They constantly delight in the True Dharma; their inner minds are tranquil, they are free from drowsiness, and they awaken to the falsity of phenomena.
Seeking the supreme Dharma, they attain thorough understanding and profound faith.
Just as the myriad stars dwell in the void, their various lusters being magnificent, beautiful, and exquisite;

so too are the bodies of the devas, their palaces, and their towers—adorned with all manner of wondrous jewels, radiating light, possessing perfect forms and characteristics beyond compare, such that words cannot fully describe them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The mundane and the supramundane, All are created by the mind;
Just like a skilled painter, Who achieves mastery through his craft."
"Immersed in the three realms of existence, liberation likewise arises from the mind;
like a silkworm binding itself, one is deludedly attached to various sensory objects.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All sentient beings, transmigrating through the three realms of existence, are deluded and defiled by their environments,
bound by mental distraction, and remain unawakened to the various true paths."
They do not understand what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is true and what is false, nor what is sublime wisdom and what is wrong attachment.

Surrounded by a vast multitude of asura retinues and musicians, they delight in play and sport; infatuated and immersed in sensual indulgence, they abandon themselves to licentiousness, never ceasing their dissipation.

“Bhikṣus, you should know: observe those [realms] and do not give rise to deluded attachment. You should cultivate generosity and precepts to guard their purity; thus you will obtain the palaces of the devas, the five desires, parents, kinsmen and friends, rare jewels, and wealth and goods—all fully provided;
as well as various treasuries for inexhaustible enjoyment, beloved by all.”

“Bhikṣus, you should know that a person of wisdom is able to guard the pure precepts, is able to proceed upon the path of goodness, and is able to praise the most supreme, incomparable, tranquil peace and happiness. Such a person is able to remain free from drowning; the faculties and physical form they obtain are excellent and complete, radiating brilliance, and their praises are inexhaustible.”
The observance of the precepts is supreme: neither water, fire, nor violent thieves can invade or destroy it;
the observance of the precepts is supreme: it enables one to leave behind lowly births and proceed toward parinirvāṇa;
the observance of the precepts is supreme: merit increases, and one is honored and respected.
Guarding the precepts is supreme: its beautiful fame spreads far and wide, and all who hear it rejoice;
guarding the precepts is supreme: greed and anger are distanced, and afflictions become slight;
guarding the precepts is supreme: one swiftly realizes parinirvāṇa.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; one will always abide among humans and devas.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; one achieves samādhi.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; one can pacify all obstacles.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; body and mind are peaceful and joyful.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; merit is firm and stable.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; one is far removed from the animal realm.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; it is superior to the abandonment of nakedness.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; it brings mastery over gardens and groves.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; it results in the perfection of one's retinue.
Guarding the precepts is most supreme; it purifies the three karmas.
Guarding the precepts is most supreme; it brings joy to all the devas.
Guarding the precepts is most supreme; all one's aspirations are fulfilled.
The upholding of the precepts is supreme, for it ensures constant encounter with virtuous friends;
the upholding of the precepts is supreme, for it brings one far away from famine and all forms of fear;
the upholding of the precepts is supreme, for it causes one to remain entirely free from the three calamities and the eight difficulties.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; it is like a sharp tool capable of severing unwholesome states.
Guarding the precepts is supreme; it is vast and sovereign, free from all fetters.
Monks, you should know that by guarding the precepts with purity, one attains such immeasurable merits as these.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who guards the precepts with purity, they will be born by transformation among the devas, constantly dwelling in palaces and towers made of mani-jewels, amidst gardens, groves, and bathing pools. They will delight in play within these most exquisite realms, observing them without end, possessing sovereign mastery and unimpeded freedom."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The six sense faculties take various objects as their conditions; Delusion and karma arise from this.
Sinking and wallowing in the three evil realms, The cycle continues without interruption.”
"Just as a wild fire is able to extinguish all fuel and wood,
so too is the skillful cessation of the root-consciousness when it conditions its objects.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is another person who violates the pure precepts yet seeks the superior retribution of peace and happiness in the human or celestial realms, they will ultimately be unable to obtain it;
all their palaces, treasures, and retinues shall likewise be dispersed."

“Bhikṣus, you should know: if a wise person guards the precepts with purity, they will abandon the three miserable realms and dwell eternally among the devas. They shall traverse and sport upon stairways of the seven treasures, enjoying sovereign bliss;
their precious jewels are immeasurable, bringing joy to all who behold them. In the most excellent groves, they revel with ease;
their bodies radiate light like lamps and candles as they walk through their palaces. Such various, exquisite, and supreme rewards are inexhaustible and beyond praise.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Diligently guard the precepts; bathe yourself in purity, so that you may be spacious and unimpeded in all places."
They are constantly adorned with celestial garlands and necklaces; celestial music plays in uninterrupted succession, and they experience every kind of pleasure at all times.
Supreme and exquisite objects appear as soon as they are thought of, and the gardens are lush with various flowers and fruits.
Furthermore, one should respectfully make offerings to and purely serve all beings, whether humans or devas.
"Therefore, bhikṣus! Guard the pure precepts;
out of compassion for those suffering sentient beings in the three evil realms, deliver them and lead them to liberation."
Furthermore, if there is a person who constantly practices giving to all sentient beings suffering from hardship, hunger, and poverty;
and who, moreover, abstains from taking life and extensively cultivates various virtues, they will obtain retribution in the heavens.
They remain far removed from perverse desires, constantly give rise to right faith, and delight in parinirvāṇa.
They do not covet worldly gain, fame, or anything pertaining to wine, sensual forms, or other things that are illusory and unreal; they distance themselves from all such things entirely.
"Regarding all sentient beings, one should abandon transgressions, karma, and afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Results arise from karma, just as a tree grows depending on its roots."
Or karma acts as mutual conditions, continuing on without end.
Good and evil are created by the mind; like a shadow that never leaves the body, they follow.
When honey and poison are mixed together, the resulting decay and harm are just the same.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, if there is a person whose heavenly merit is exhausted and the signs of decline appear before them, all their kinsmen and retinue will completely abandon them."
Just as when a lamp is about to go out, its light inevitably dims, so it is with the gods.

At this time, as their merit and lifespan are about to end, they are oppressed by manifold sufferings; bound by anxiety and affliction, their terror is immeasurable. Their bodies and minds are tormented, and various defilements arise.
Before long, they will inevitably reach the end of their lives and, according to their past karma, fall into the three miserable realms;
or, if born among humans, they will transmigrate without ceasing, like sentient beings bound by shackles and fetters, sinking into the various states of existence and failing to attain liberation.
They confuse right faith, distance themselves from tranquility, and associate with evil friends as well as former enemies.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that such wandering through the realms and destinies within the three worlds arises entirely because delusion and karma have not been subdued and eliminated, nor has there been true awakening."

Driven by these karmas and afflictions, sentient beings are scorched without ceasing, just as firewood being consumed by flames blazes with ever-increasing intensity; this fire of the three poisons that burns away all wholesome virtues is likewise so.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that this greed, hatred, and delusion are like a great river that sweeps away sentient beings, preventing them from escaping.
Furthermore, these [afflictions] such as greed are like snares that bind sentient beings, so that they cannot attain liberation;
moreover, these [afflictions] such as greed are also like dust and grime that defile sentient beings, so that they cannot attain purity.”
Therefore, the wise should eliminate and sever [these faults].

Furthermore, if there are those who protect the Buddha’s pure precepts and practice generosity, abandon flattery and deception, subdue and eliminate greed and delusion until they gradually become faint, and thoroughly understand all phenomena so as not to give rise to attachment.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is a person whose afflictions such as greed arise as the seeds of suffering, and they are unable to subdue and eliminate them, nor can they escape the various sufferings of the three realms of existence, it is like a thirsty person drinking salt water; their thirst cannot be relieved.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know: contemplate the unsurpassed bliss of liberation and proceed toward parinirvāṇa.
Cultivate meditative concentration to extinguish all defilements; do not cling to fetters that lead to falling into hell and undergoing manifold sufferings while straying from the right path.”

The devas and asuras all abandon him; the nāgas become enraged, bringing unseasonable winds and rains; the four seasons do not proceed in their proper order, the grain does not ripen, and the people suffer from famine.
All happiness has utterly departed; beloved palaces, gardens, and most exquisite realms have been destroyed and no longer exist.
The treasures and wealth in the storehouses have all been scattered and dissipated.
They harm one another, deluded and inverted, lacking any sense of awakening.
They have never practiced that which is of supreme benefit;
they slander the true Dharma of the Three Vehicles as being non-existent.
Deluded within the three realms, they falsely cling to what is unreal as being ultimate reality.
They even recklessly misjudge the sun, moon, and stars.
Furthermore, they falsely deny the existence of all the merits and demerits possessed by sentient beings.
Unable to comprehend the nectar-like True Dharma, they constantly harbor hatred and envy, treating it as if it were a poisonous enemy to be loathed, rejected, and abandoned.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that deluded sentient beings perceive pleasure within the sufferings of the world; they conceive the impure to be pure, take refuge in heterodox paths, and falsely cling to the most evil states as supreme, delighting in their cultivation."
Failing to comprehend impermanence and other such truths, they falsely conceive of erroneous dharmas as supreme.
Delighting in them, they apply themselves with resolute diligence; yet, since no true benefit exists, they cannot escape saṃsāra, remaining forever subject to bitter suffering.

The wise should observe this without falling into deluded attachment; they should comprehend its falsity, discern right from wrong, awaken from their intoxicated confusion, and ensure their minds remain undisturbed.

At that time, the great assembly surrounded the World-Honored One; hearing the Dharma, they were filled with joy, delight, and exultation. Having cast off their fetters, they gazed up at the Tathāgata, their eyes never wavering for a moment.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"Just as Mount Sumeru is adorned with the four jewels,
Encircled on all sides by seven golden mountains, And surrounded by the eight seas, serene and pure."
The World-Honored One’s marks are peerless; his wisdom and principle transcend all verbal expression.
Having fulfilled the myriad practices through cultivation, the virtues of the three bodies are perfected as the fruit.
As humans and devas look up to you with longing, we pray that you will explain the causes and conditions of your past lives.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had praised the Buddha with verses, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The deities of the desire realm and the form realm differ in their physical dimensions and merit."
"We pray that the Buddha will expound this teaching for the benefit of those in the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Listen attentively, and I shall speak for you.
If there is another person who upholds the pure precepts, skillfully guards the sense faculties so as not to commit transgressions, and keeps the three karmas pure;
Toward all sentient beings, they cultivate compassion and benefit them, diligently practicing skillful means and abandoning distraction to seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Regarding the causes thus cultivated, whether superior, middling, or inferior, there are differences; the resulting fruits are likewise distinct.
Even as for the external vessel-world, its palaces and adornments, their heights and forms, all differ according to past causes and conditions.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By guarding the pure precepts and practicing generosity, one constantly dwells among the devas; having abandoned all defilements, all fetters are suppressed and eliminated so that they do not arise."
Regarding those various devas, within their own bodies and the external environment, they take delight in them and seek them out; they do not give rise to disparagement, destruction, or revulsion.
After the end of their lives, they will certainly be reborn there, and the superiority or inferiority of the retribution they obtain will vary according to their causes.
“Bhikṣus, you should know: by guarding the pure precepts of the Buddha, the palaces of the devas are eternally and spontaneously joyful;
by guarding the pure precepts of the Buddha, one abandons all suffering and attains liberation free from defilement;
by guarding the pure precepts of the Buddha, one is eternally adorned with celestial garlands and necklaces.”
By guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one possesses the exquisite fragrance of the *utpala* flower that is pleasing to the mind;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one experiences the inexhaustible joy and tranquility of the most sublime realms;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, constantly provide assistance and protection.
One upholds the Buddha’s pure precepts, adorned with all manner of jewels because they are free from all defilements;
one upholds the Buddha’s pure precepts, wherein various celestial flowers of wondrous colors bloom and manifest according to the mind's mastery;
one upholds the Buddha’s pure precepts, whereby subtle and exquisite fragrant breezes bring inexhaustible delight to the mind.
By guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one enjoys rooms, gardens, and groves according to one's heart's desire;

by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one obtains various *mālu* flowers, *campaka* flowers, and *kettaka* flowers, which emit a most supreme and peerless wondrous fragrance that is ever present before one;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one remains far removed from all calamities.
By guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, the seeds of goodness increase;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, all conditions for violating the precepts are completely distanced;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, the practice of patience is brought to fulfillment.
By guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, one achieves and manifests the sublime jewel-stairway;
by guarding the Buddha’s pure precepts, all varieties of craftsmanship and delightful requisites are fully accomplished.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that by guarding the pure precepts of the Buddha, one obtains such fruits in future lives.
Just as a painter can bring to completion all manner of mundane and supramundane forms, so too is it with the guarding of the precepts:
in future lives, everything will be accomplished according to one’s wishes.”

"Furthermore, if there are those who violate the pure precepts, they shall, in future lives, sink into the evil realms and undergo various sufferings, being deprived of the lovely environments of humans and devas."
Just as a painted image can be destroyed by wind, rain, smoke, and dust,
so too can the stains of greed, hatred, and the like destroy pure ethical discipline, and cause one to abandon both worldly and supramundane desirable fruits.
"Furthermore, monks! The various afflictions such as greed can destroy sentient beings,
yet they can also cause all wholesome karma to increase."
All unwholesome karmas are like the fierce flames of a worldly fire that grow ever stronger and can destroy firewood.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the faculties and consciousnesses of sentient beings grasp at the six sense objects, becoming deluded and failing to understand."
Bound by the fetters of false attachment to objective realms, they give rise to greed and hatred;
various karmas follow in succession, causing them to revolve through the various states of existence and undergo immeasurable suffering, unable to escape.
The various poisons of craving leave the deluded ignorant and unawakened.
The fire of craving blazes fiercely, destroying all manner of virtues as well as delightful palaces, groves, and ponds; all the exquisite fruits are utterly scattered and ruined.
Lāsakā possessed supreme and wondrous merit and retribution; his treasuries were filled with immeasurable precious jewels, and he enjoyed himself with sovereign ease.
His parents and kinsmen possessed the highest merit and virtue, rare in this world, and lived in unhindered happiness.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if there is a person who cultivates the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they will be fully endowed with wealth and property in future lives and remain free from all forms of ruin.
The perfection of giving is most supreme, bringing joy and sovereignty;
the practice of giving is most supreme, such that its karmic reward follows one like a shadow, never departing.”
The practice of giving is most supreme; it is beloved by humans and devas, and brings about adornment and joy.
The practice of giving is most supreme; it enables one to leave behind poverty.
The practice of giving is most supreme; it prevents stinginess from arising.
The practice of giving is supreme; it can subdue ignorance and lead one out of the three miserable realms.
The practice of giving is supreme; those who see it rejoice.
The practice of giving is supreme; it ensures that the sense faculties are complete and unimpaired.
The practice of giving is supreme; animals delight in seeing it.
The practice of giving is supreme; it brings one far from love and hatred.
The practice of giving is supreme; one is not born in the borderlands.
The practice of giving is supreme, bringing joy to all the devas;
the practice of giving is supreme, liberating one from the bonds of suffering;
the practice of giving is supreme, transcending saṃsāra.
The practice of giving is supreme; it brings mastery over enjoyments.
The practice of giving is supreme; it enables one to proceed toward the three vehicles and attain ultimate liberation. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!
One should observe that the various sufferings of saṃsāra involve manifold oppressions and should cultivate weary detachment from them.
One should scrutinize them with discernment as being non-ultimate, impermanent, and subject to decay—like a dream, like a flame, or like the unripened core of a plantain tree;

they are not real. Even all the realms of the form and formless worlds are illusory and unreal, lacking any ultimate reality. One should cultivate weary detachment toward them, rather than becoming attached to them, falsely regarding them as supreme, or allowing the mind to find delight in them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Parinirvāṇa is blissful and free from all marks; its essence is neither one nor many, nor does it belong to the three periods of time. It is neither this nor that, free from all fetters, and is ultimately perfect.”
"You should pursue this; you must not abandon it.
It is sovereign and unimpeded, tranquil and untainted; you should swiftly realize it.
