At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly, saying: "The merit you have performed is well done;
may it be protected, increased, and bring you joy as you wish."
Then he spoke these verses:
"Having performed the three kinds of wholesome deeds, With the three types and three causal conditions,
In three stages and across three levels, One attains the three virtues and the three great fruits."
The gift of non-killing is supreme; if you take delight in this Dharma, you shall attain true patience and be born among all the heavens.
There, you will possess celestial palaces that follow your body, and you shall enjoy infinite bliss.
If a person delights in what is unwholesome, there will be no peace in their place of birth;
ensnared by the increase of false dharmas, how can they achieve liberation?
By performing wholesome deeds as humans and devas, one perfumes and cultivates them within the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
"When that karma ripens into its fruit, one is born in the realms of humans or devas;
finding joy and delight therein, the mind dwells naturally in peace and happiness.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again, saying:
“You all possess great merit and have been born in the celestial realms to enjoy heavenly bliss; according to the superiority or inferiority of your respective fruits of merit, each is distinct.

If you perform various kinds of meritorious deeds, they will perfume the consciousness within your bodies, so that upon being reborn in the celestial realms, you shall obtain various kinds of happiness.”
All such trees, groves, flowers, and fruits there bring delight to the human mind;
upon entering that forest, the celestial birds there utter sounds that are a joy for all to hear, and they speak these verses for the sake of the deva-son:
"Welcome, O virtuous and wise one! You have practiced sublime goodness in your past lives."
By steadfastly maintaining the sevenfold discipline, one achieves the most supreme fruit;
born within those celestial realms, one receives the retribution of divine bliss.
By extensively upholding the prohibitive precepts, one attains liberation from the suffering of cyclic existence.
Just as through the purity of one's precepts, one is moved by the sublime and wondrous ponds of the heavens to bathe therein at will;
furthermore, flowers of purple-gold rain down, scattering upon one's body.
And that pool of merit: by means of the seeds of those precepts, one guards against wrongdoing in every thought-moment;
thus, the supreme and wondrous pleasures among the gods are enjoyed according to one's will.
If a person’s mind is resolute and they guard the prohibitive precepts,
when they are born in that celestial realm, their happiness will be boundless.
Adorned with these precepts, they shall attain the fruit of the Sugata.
And thus experience the bliss of liberation;
the evil of breaking the precepts is as deep as a sword, fire, or poison.
Therefore, firmly uphold the precepts and cultivate the wealth of the Dharma through giving, remaining far removed from the violation of prohibitions.
Karma has superior, middling, and inferior degrees, and the resulting fruits are likewise so; now,
having attained this body of supreme retribution, you constantly wear a garland of radiance,
enjoy the various pleasures of the heavens, and possess a pure body free from defilement.
If one commits evil deeds, the bitter fruits will entwine one's own body;
transmigrating through successive rebirths, one undergoes sinking and delusion, with birth and death having no end.
Since you have been born here, you enjoy the pleasures of the celestial hosts.
When wandering through the various gardens and groves, do not become attached to heedlessness;
for the fault of dissipation is profound, as the Tathāgata has always taught.
Therefore, among the three poisons, heedlessness is the most grave.
Vigorous effort is like nectar; the mind and crown of the head become naturally cool.
One forever transcends the wheel of birth and death, reaching at last the shore of Bodhi.
At that time, I, the Tathāgata, proclaimed these subtle and wondrous words.
Abandoning the self, practice swiftly; do not cling to inverted perceptions.
If one acts in opposition, the various afflictions such as craving will arise;
severing the conditions for liberation, one will drift and sink in the ocean of suffering.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, swiftly proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall; all the celestial musicians and the entire host of devas likewise came to the Sudharmā Hall.
Having arrived, they engaged in various forms of entertainment and play.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, observed their amusements and perceived that the celestial hosts were attached to falsehoods and increasing their afflictions; he then spoke these verses:
"Amidst false objects of experience, They crave with no sense of satiety."
Sentient beings are deeply deluded and attached, increasing all manner of afflictions;
bound by sensory objects to their faculties and consciousness, they are like poison hidden within food—
when it later digests, they suffer confusion and lack any peace.
Without before, after, or middle; not belonging to this life nor to future lives—when causes and conditions meet, who can avoid the retribution of karma?
At that time, after Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these verses, he further addressed him, saying:
"Even if one is young and possesses great strength, there is no certainty of long life; the four marks of existence shift and change, swiftly leading to dispersal and extinction."
They manifest as pleasure, yet lack any real intrinsic nature; when the sensation of pleasure exhausts, they oppress both body and mind, leaving no moment of peace or security.
You must not place your trust in delusion, ignorance, and deceit; if you become stained by attachment toward all sensory objects, it will lead to great suffering in the future.
Just as a blazing fire consumes grass and leaves, so too does attachment to sensory objects increase all manner of faults.
Scorched and boiled by the fires of affliction, they turn their backs on the Right Path; when the signs of decline appear, they fall from the celestial realms.
Therefore, I now instruct you all to sever the afflictions and eliminate delusion;

all you celestial hosts, from this point forward, shall constantly perform what is beneficial for the practice of the supreme Dharma, cultivating it with firm resolve, so that you may later attain the supreme peace and bliss of tranquility.
Do not now be negligent or arrogant; quickly cultivate the field of merit.
In this very life, you shall obtain the most supreme retribution, which will be satisfying and inexhaustible.
If you commit various evil deeds that follow you, you will fall from the celestial palaces and sink into the miserable realms; all your palaces and towers will then completely vanish.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing that the son of the gods had passed away in an instant and fallen into an evil destiny, spoke this verse:
“Subtle and fragrant lotus flowers, Arising in various ways upon the mountain peaks,
Supreme and pleasing jewels, Adorning every place.”
Flowing springs and bathing pools, Trees of various colored flowers and fruits,
And kalpa-trees of purple and gold— Upon these gather flocks of wondrous birds,
Constantly emitting subtle and exquisite sounds, Delighting the hosts of devas.
Stainless lapis lazuli jewels, interspersed with golden light, form most excellent and wondrous towers and terraces, adorned and ever pleasing to the mind.
Beings do not depart from them; how could they know these are but illusory transformations?
Like bubbles and like foam, like lightning and like floating clouds,
and also like a city of Gandharvas— they vanish and perish in an instant.
If false imaginings give rise to craving, one falls onto the path of saṃsāra.
The poison of deluded attachment is like fire;
it incinerates the roots of goodness, diminishes the hosts of devas, and removes all bodhi.
He further addressed them, saying:
"If a deva is foolish and deluded by attachment to humans, he will be overcome by devas, asuras, rākṣasas, and the like; subsequently, he will fall into hell.
Furthermore, becoming a nāga or a serpent, he will be far removed from the various devas and dwell long within the three realms, bound as if by ropes, lacking any autonomy."

If one is free from delusion and craving, attains clear and thorough understanding, benefits sentient beings, takes refuge in the Buddha-way, forever transcends the mundane world, severs the link of craving for existence, and attains all-knowledge;

if one is impartial and unimpeded, attains the three liberations, realizes suffering and emptiness to reach the limit of reality, distances oneself from saṃsāra, does not undergo further existence, and is untainted by form, fragrance, flavor, or touch.

At that time, the Lord of the Devas, seeing the many hosts of devas whose every thought was impermanent and whose faults were increasing, gave rise to deep compassion. He spoke these words of truth and uttered this verse:
"When such a celestial path comes to an end, One sinks and wanders for hundreds of thousands of kalpas;
Like a whirling wheel of fire, When will birth and death ever reach their end?"
Seeing others undergo impermanence, yet not observing this within oneself,
when one’s own life eventually comes to an end, the suffering and harm will be exactly the same.
If one abandons the defiled mind and does not cling to sensory objects, [one will not suffer].
Neither birth nor death can invade it; one dwells eternally in true, tranquil bliss.
If one violates the precepts and conduct, it is like a drunken man consuming medicinal poison.
It is not the armies of Māra or the host of Death that cause this; when bound by such fetters, who can provide deliverance?
With fine dust covering one’s face, what does one’s own mind perceive?
When life ends and one lies within the forest, who awakens to the fact that it all stems from craving?
If one gives rise to craving, one dwells together with suffering and impermanence.
Forever dwelling in birth and death, manifesting as separated from peace and joy;
with great evils not severed or removed, saṃsāra is obtained from this,
just as a violent and evil wind can blow away the leaves from the mountain peaks.
Through one's own karma one attains birth in heaven, where one personally experiences the fruits of delight;
by maintaining pure precepts without delusion, one is fully satisfied with peace and happiness.
Greed and folly invite a fall, like smoke rising from fire.
"Afterward, one falls into hell oneself; the retribution of karma is likewise.
At that time, there was a deva named Upacāru who, by the power of his past wholesome karma, was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There was a bhikṣu who served as his celestial king and spoke this verse:
“If one performs various kinds of karma, And falsely grasps at objects everywhere,
Through the power of mental delusion, All such karma is brought to fruition.”
Because the preceding mind is supreme, the subsequent mind arises in succession;
drawing it forth without interval, the causes within the three realms are inexhaustible.
All bodies resulting from karmic retribution cannot be found apart from the mind.
Therefore, by subduing the mind, one shall obtain inexhaustible fruits.

You should swiftly and diligently apply yourself to cultivation; by taming the mind and abandoning attachment and delusion, you will fulfill all virtues according to your heart's desire and ultimately attain peace and happiness.
If the mind is constantly subdued, faults will never increase;
the wise who skillfully subdue the mind cannot be harmed by any suffering.
If the mind encounters that suffering, the suffering of suffering will continue in succession.
Within all realms of experience, one receives the retribution of a lightened mind.
Whether gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, ghosts, rākṣasas, or others,
they do not depart from this single mind.

The three realms of existence arise from one’s own mind; hell, the human realm, and the heavens all follow the mind in producing transgression or merit, drifting and sinking as they are carried along by the current.
When one destroys wholesome causes through delusion in the face of sensory objects, ignorance and craving are born.
Abiding in suffering, vast and boundless, they sink and find it hard to emerge.
The mind is difficult to tame and possesses great power; it rushes about as swiftly as the wind.
O Divine Eye, do not take form as your object; the characteristics of consciousness are all like this.
The wise one, well-disciplined, Is far removed from the bonds of Māra;
Having crossed over the river of birth and death, He swiftly reaches the further shore.
Doubt is crooked and unrighteous; This bottomless evil is difficult to restrain.
The manifold subtle movements do not abide even for a single moment.
Their modes of activity are so dense as to be difficult to fathom; bodiless yet present everywhere, who in this world can lead them?
Who was it that went away?
Deeply hidden within the dharmas, one performs bodily karma;
though the outward manifestations of action are seen to differ, the corresponding dharma is not perceived.
What is the difficulty of subduing?
It is formless and without physical characteristics; though it is base and harmful to sentient beings, it perceives objects as clearly as the eye.
Although one sees its good and evil deeds, it is like a conjured phantom.
Its fundamental nature is difficult to fathom; who can perceive its coming and going?
It draws along all living beings, causing them to perpetually transmigrate through the various realms of existence.
A sharp sword cannot cut it; even a fierce fire cannot sever it by burning.
The minds of all sentient beings are such that the power of karma manifests in this way;
the ropes of karma are firm and bind all living beings.
The three natures are not constant; in an instant they may be wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, accompanied by equanimity, they cling to the gates of the six sense faculties.
Seeking falsely among sensory objects, because of their defiled attachment to the world, they do not realize the law of arising and ceasing;
it is like a mirror that only reflects what stands before it.
"And do not fail to take heed for the future.
At that time, having heard those words of the bhikṣu—how he had formerly practiced pure goodness and now obtained this superior body—the devaputra spoke these verses:
"In the past, you cultivated a tranquil and sublime mind, And carefully guarded your conduct of the precepts."
By means of these subtle and wondrous causes, one dwells in the path of peace and happiness.
Those who skillfully guard and uphold the precepts, warding off what is wrong and giving rise to discipline,
shall sever all delusions and realize the bliss of perfect nirvana.
The precepts possess great majestic power; they can transcend the suffering of all realms of existence.
Even at the time when life comes to an end, one has no fear of the evil paths.
No one can save one from the evil paths; the power of the precepts is the supreme savior.
If there are those who uphold the precepts, all myriad virtues will rely upon them;
as a future result, they shall be born in the heavens and forever leave behind all perils and hardships.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha are the teachers whom all within the three realms revere.
At that time, the sons of the gods prostrated themselves, casting their bodies to the ground in homage, and gave rise to a heart of deep reverence.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, felt redoubled joy and, with the deepest praise, spoke these verses:
"Having liberated himself from the poisons of greed and hatred, He is a kinsman and a friend to all living beings."
Able to reach the further shore, I now take refuge and pay homage to you.
Having subdued the loss of folly, unconditioned and peerless,
honored by all the multitudes, I now take refuge and pay homage to you.
At that time, there were various flying birds among those devas; some soared up and down in the air, while others gathered at the jeweled ponds to sport within the water.
There were also sons of gods who, seeking pleasure and indulgence, roamed together with the winged creatures; addicted to sensual delights, they felt no fear of the evil realms.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke these verses for the sake of those deva sons:
"Animals indulge in sensual pleasures, Sporting at will in their folly and delusion;
The hosts of devas are likewise so, Equal to those classes of winged birds."
The True Teacher has declared: "Your minds are inverted;
you do not fear sinful karma, but instead indulge in pleasure and remain attached to the world.
If devas possess sinful karma, they shall fall into the hells."
The power of karma is such a poison that the wise always keep it at a distance.
Those of meager merit and little wisdom perceive only immediate sensual pleasures;
failing to reflect upon them, they bring about the fruits of various sufferings.
If there is a person of wisdom who clearly perceives all evils,
seeking to sever all karmic misdeeds for the benefit of all living beings;
since sinful karma gives rise to all suffering, through superior causes one attains liberation from bondage.
Good and evil deeds differ, and their retributive results are likewise so.
To mistake suffering for pleasure through delusion is to seek security that can never be found;
one who possesses wisdom should not commit wrongs, for before long they shall reach the state of quiescence.
Skillfully cultivating the tranquility of all karmas and gathering roots of goodness through expedient means,
samādhi will manifest before you, and you shall swiftly reach the stage of non-arising.
Do not again linger among the animals, sporting in gardens and groves.
If laziness increases further, one will later fall among the species of flying birds.
Furthermore, if one lacks even a modicum of wisdom and cannot distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome karma,
one will likewise be reborn as a hungry ghost, an asura, or even in hell.
They are able to discern karma and also penetrate its retribution;
regarding all karmas, they profoundly exhaust their impure and tranquil characteristics.
Day and night they are constantly diligent, contemplating the three gates of liberation.
One shall never fall into hell, but will ultimately attain peace and happiness.
O Devaputra, you should know this: one’s own joy is accomplished through one’s own goodness;
from one’s own delusion arises one’s own suffering. Suffering and happiness do not exist apart from the mind.
One should distance oneself from the past, for one is attached to various sensory objects;
blinded by heedlessness and delusion, one fails to perceive the urging of the King of Death,
sinking into hell with boundless suffering and distress.
At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens of exquisite and dignified appearance, possessing sovereign mastery over their desires, singing and sporting amidst those groves.
There was a flying bird that, knowing the celestial being’s past virtuous deeds, spoke this verse:
“By diligently cultivating virtuous karma in the past, You have now been reborn in the heavens;
But had you practiced unwholesome causes, You would have sunk again into the evil realms.”
Since karmic retribution is certain, all devas are equal;
whether they experience happiness or suffering, you should now know this.
Attachment is the root of harm, and the ropes of karma bind one accordingly.
Whirling on without end, it returns through the power of the cord of karma.
Reaching upward to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and extending downward to the three miserable realms,
its coming and going is as swift as the wind, and the number of births is like falling rain.
Cycling through the various realms of existence, it has been thus for a beginningless time.
If the human mind is tranquil, as still and clear as water,
and free from obstruction like space, one attains the supreme bliss.
The five consciousnesses take external objects as their conditions; The three evil karmas draw one along in succession.
When even a single dharma is abandoned and exhausted, One cannot be born in the heavenly realms.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and the poison of lying— These are constantly the companions of one’s evil path.
Like being burned by a blazing fire, the wise should observe this;
true patience and loving-kindness are the virtuous spiritual friends who transcend the world.
If one draws near to and cultivates them, one shall attain the fruits of the three heavens.
Subduing perverse and distracted thoughts, And carefully guarding against craving for sensory contact and the like,
One will subsequently be born in heaven through meditative concentration, Accomplishing the fruits of pure karma.
If one does not seek liberation From the karma of birth and death, [one remains bound].
"When the Yama-killer demon arrives, how can one remain far removed from it?
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again:
"If there are sentient beings who do not fear any evils, yet whose minds are stained by attachments in all places;
Because of such defiled attachment, wisdom is obscured.

They engage in false speech, frivolous talk, deception, and wicked flattery, thereby harassing and confusing sentient beings. They turn their backs on the true teaching and associate with evil teachers; they are unfilial toward their parents, and even their roots of goodness are severed, as they are bound by the cords of karma.
Like a swift arrow, one enters hell at death, where one undergoes various punishments and experiences all manner of extreme suffering without respite.
From this day forward, you must quickly abandon the conditions for the sins of birth and death; do not again become attached to them with craving.
One should carefully and thoroughly observe that the duration of one's own life is limited, whether short or long;
for all conditioned phenomena arise and perish in every moment—how could they possibly endure for long?

Like bubbles floating on water, like reflections in a mirror, like lightning in an instant, and like clouds dispersing and vanishing—when one’s heavenly merit is exhausted and one relinquishes the state of blissful experience, all signs of decay suddenly appear before one, oppressing both body and mind; how could one possibly endure this?
Therefore, I now declare to you:

"You must now practice with diligent effort, cultivate patience and gentleness, have compassion for sentient beings, guard the six sense faculties, and practice the Four Noble Truths. Do not distinguish between enemies and kin, but cultivate equanimity; increase your wisdom to penetrate the profound meaning of the Dharma; turn your back on delusion to illuminate the truth, and guide yourself toward meditative concentration."
"When karma and afflictions are exhausted, future existence does not arise, and one attains liberation through both [aspects].
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to restate this meaning, further spoke in verse:
"Thus, regarding the twelve bases—the six objects and the six faculties—"
When consciousness and the other aggregates arise and perish, their conjunction constitutes delusive conceptualization.
The wise person skillfully cultivates the mind, does not dwell upon dharmas such as form,
and enters the gate of tranquility, where all is profoundly still and devoid of even a single characteristic.
Because they diligently seek tranquility, they do not fall into the realm of Māra;
with this serene and wondrous mind, they maintain constant mindfulness.
If one practices such wisdom, how could afflictions and suffering arise?
Within the three periods of time, they are sovereign and free from fear;
the bonds of affliction are naturally released, and the stains of transgression cannot defile them.
Their eye of wisdom attains perfect clarity, and they dwell eternally in the practice of true stillness.
Even the celestial bodies, despite their great happiness, are still crushed by the defilements of sin;
how much more so for deluded human beings—why do they extensively create the ten evil karmas?
If a person cultivates wisdom, they will thoroughly understand the causes of both sin and merit.
"Fearing that death may invade one's karma, one shall forever emerge from the root of suffering.
At that time, Śakra, having previously heard from the World-Honored One concerning the matters of the evil realms, immediately proclaimed to the assembly of devas:
"The Buddha said:"
"If a person attains liberation from the root of the sins of birth and death, they will constantly encounter virtuous friends and plant various roots of goodness.
If they are born in the celestial realms, they will experience sublime bliss, with palaces so magnificently adorned that their karmic rewards are immeasurable.

Yet, if they do not fear the evil paths and remain greedily attached to worldly pleasures, then when their merit and goodness are exhausted, they will inevitably fall—just as a lamp or candle requires oil; once the oil is spent, the flame is extinguished."
Having thus fallen, they are swiftly blown and whirled about by the winds of karma, circling through the world without ceasing.

If those who possess wisdom are in accord with right concentration, the ropes of ignorance and karma cannot move them; it is like the fibers of a lotus root, which cannot move Mount Sumeru even when pulled.
At that time, having heard the Lord of Devas preach this Dharma, that deity spoke these verses in praise of the Lord of Devas:
"You have now preached this Dharma, Which extinguishes and removes all obstacles.
Relying upon the words of the Lord of Devas, I abide in fearlessness."
To all those living beings, you act as a compassionate father;
You proclaim the city of Nirvana, enabling them to attain benefit and joy.
The Dharma is fundamentally without discrimination; O Lord of Devas, you are well able to proclaim it.
"Now that I have encountered a true teacher, I shall attain the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the Lord of Devas spoke again, saying:
"Do not give rise to greedy attachment toward worldly wealth and goods."
If a person abandons the arising of wisdom, or conversely becomes attached to it, they will destroy their roots of goodness;
the seven kinds of noble wealth will gradually vanish, and for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they will sink and wallow in the evil realms.
Furthermore, worldly wealth is not enduring; it can be seized by the power of water, fire, thieves, kings, and the like.
However, that which is the wealth of the Dharma can never be destroyed by calamities such as water or fire.
"O assembly of devas, although you possess power, have your faculties intact, and your bodies are endowed with radiance,
when the signs of decline appear, you will give rise to grief and affliction, fall through the void for more than a hundred thousand yojanas, and enter into the miserable realms."
At that time, Śakra spoke these verses:
"Just as you now possess such great happiness and immeasurable wealth and honor,
should the signs of decline appear before you, you will certainly sink into the evil realms."
Just as the actions performed in the present, The fruits of those actions arise accordingly;
As the characteristics of the action are excellent, So too is the ripened fruit.
Actions are categorized as superior, middling, or inferior, And likewise within the categories of good and evil.
When that existence with its retribution is formed, the superior and inferior are likewise so.
You all should reflect deeply: though physical strength and form may be supreme, one cannot escape birth and death; how then could one not fall?
Just as when seeds such as wheat are scorched by a great fire, they are destroyed at the very moment of burning; how then could a sprout arise?
This body, which is hollow, empty, false, and deceptive, is subject to the rapid flux of the four marks of existence.
Just as a lamp produces a flame that does not abide for even a single moment, so too is the nature of the mind: illusory and devoid of reality.
Constantly pursued by the increase of outflows (*āsrava*), how can one attain peace and happiness?
"Abandon delusive objects; do not cherish your own body.
You shall certainly escape saṃsāra and swiftly reach the other shore.
At that time, the bird belonging to that deity spoke again:

“We currently dwell in the Utpala Grove; within that grove there is a great bathing pool where many red lotuses grow, fragrant for a long time. The bodies and wings of the birds are variegated in color like the seven precious gems;
their eyes possess radiance and their voices are exquisite, as they sport and delight in that forest for a long time.”
Observing that the devaputra was deeply attached and intoxicated, he spoke these verses:
"I am always delighted by pleasure, and the same is true for the love of gods and humans.
Though gods differ from birds, their passionate attachment is no different."
If one cannot maintain the practice of the Dharma, how can one attain liberation?
If gods and others were like this, what would distinguish them from birds?
Now I further tell you all: do not be attached to the pleasures of the five desires.
By practicing the sublime Dharma, one shall attain great liberation.
The sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death shall never harm one’s body;
both the bodies of devas and those of birds shall equally obtain wholesome benefit.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke again:
"If there is a wise person who is free from defilement and pure, even though worldly sins and stains pervade this heaven, they cannot adhere to him."
"Why is this? Because those wise ones are able to understand birth and the causes and conditions of suffering;
furthermore, they harbor no attachment or longing for their celestial friends, acquaintances, or beloved kinsmen."
"You gods are deluded and ignorant; stained by craving and unable to leave saṃsāra, you are no different from those flying birds.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are addicted to drinking alcohol, incurring a great many transgressions."
Why is this so? It is because the mind-consciousness of those sentient beings is deluded and confused, leading them to frequently break and violate the precepts;

though the power of the alcohol may have subsided, the karmic retribution does not perish. They continue to cycle through the five realms of existence without interruption, and among all sins, this is the most predominant. Even for ten million *koṭis* of eons, they will wander incessantly, sinking into the evil destinies and bound by afflictions—so it was spoken by the Buddha.
At that time, within the garden of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, there was a Hall of the Sublime Dharma, exquisitely adorned with various kinds of rare jewels.
Then, the hosts of devas proceeded to that hall.
At that time, Śakra surveyed the assembly of devas and spoke these verses:
"You hosts of devas, In the past you cultivated even slight merit,
And thus obtained birth within this celestial realm."
If the retribution of one's celestial rewards is exhausted, one will certainly fall into saṃsāra.
Dragging along sentient beings, one is born everywhere within the three realms and five destinies.
Examine with careful and subtle reflection: in the mere twinkling of an eye, there is arising and ceasing;
why do you not awaken to this?
Relying upon the various codes of discipline, make the seven factors of enlightenment firm and steadfast.
Diligently practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, skillfully abiding in the five faculties,
and increasing the five powers; the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts,
and those four bases of spiritual power.
Thus, without falling back, one will surely reach the city of Nirvana, Constantly experiencing the bliss of quiescent extinction.
The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness, Scroll Five.
The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Imperial Preceptor of the Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Fātian:
"One who feels no fear toward sin possesses no wisdom."
When the time of their death eventually arrives, they are constantly scorched by suffering and anguish throughout the celestial realms; who can see them as they fall?
Constantly craving sensual pleasures, they remain unaware of this.
Sensual desire gives rise to falsehood, deluding sentient beings;
it drags them down into the three miserable realms, binding them like a rope.
Birth and death are ever thus; sentient beings must seek their own benefit.
Make body, speech, and mind supple and gentle; do not allow afflictions to arise.
One must bring to rest the objects of the mind and so forth.
By increasing delusion, one falls into impermanence; failing to realize it, one is scorched by the fire of desire.
Separated from kinsmen, friends, and spiritual teachers,
From one's own flesh and blood and all attendants— When the great suffering of death arrives,
O Pāṭali, what can you say?
Like a mountain suddenly collapsing, it cannot be halted for even a moment;
in an instant, it perishes and passes away.
If one abides in all-knowledge, there is neither sin nor saṃsāra, and one ultimately emerges from the source of suffering.
The devas are ever fond of pleasure; the ocean of desire is deep and bottomless—how could there ever be a time of satisfaction?
It is like pouring clarified butter upon a fire; though their forms are adorned in every way, [they remain insatiable].
Destroying the causes for transcendence of the world, they wander through the four realms of existence.
As humans, animals, hell-beings, or hungry ghosts, their births and deaths are constant and uninterrupted;
they revolve back and forth like a potter’s wheel, the masses of beings utterly deluded.
Not understanding the nature of afflictions,
yet forever free from craving and attachment, one shall attain the supreme cause and liberation without fetters.
Various sufferings and ailments shall not invade; having subdued greed and hatred, one shall long obtain the path of peace and bliss.
No noose can bind them, as their wisdom gradually becomes perfect and luminous.
Illuminating and knowing all phenomena,
they give rise to a signless mind; free from defilement and severed from the clamor of dust,
they ultimately reach the further shore.
Regarding those objects of suffering and pleasure, one perceives them clearly as unattainable and enters great liberation.
Dwelling eternally in the abode of empty stillness, one again gives rise to a heart of compassion;
out of pity for sentient beings, one manifests the true suchness of the wisdom of suffering.
Far removed from the snares, he causes the mind to sever doubt;
forever eliminating craving and attachment, he is liberated from suffering, affliction, and fear.
Having attained the supreme wisdom, he realizes that both accumulation and dispersal are empty.
Even with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas, one still falls into impermanence;
yet this [state] can abide eternally, never losing its place in the celestial realms.
Seeing evil, one gives rise to arrogance, and fails to reflect upon one’s transgressions.
Foolish and deluded, lacking skillful means, they constantly seek happiness;
yet it is like seeking oil from a heap of sand—it can never be obtained.
If one performs sinful deeds, one will be perpetually oppressed.
The roots of sin are deep within the tree of suffering; all evils grow from it.
I declare this to be suchness, which definitively distinguishes dharma from non-dharma.
When one feels shame in the mind for having committed a transgression, subsequently there will be no further afflictions.
The benefit is vast and boundless, reaching the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*).

"If, moreover, one is deluded and does not believe or accept the Buddha’s teachings, then upon reaching impermanence, one will naturally experience suffering and affliction for countless hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta-amanas* [aeons], destroying the realms of humans and devas; the fire of the sins of impermanence will certainly burn them, and this shall not end until the kalpa is exhausted."
Gautama replied: "How could heaven endure for long?
It is like a bubble on water or a plantain tree; it possesses not even a hair’s breadth of reality, being a mere illusion that does not last."
"If one were to constantly crave this pleasure, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, that Buddha asked the assembly of devas:
"Do you understand this meaning?"
The deva’s mind was filled with joy, as if hearing the five kinds of music; he experienced great happiness and attained five merits.
He then spoke again, saying:
"There is a flying bird named *Khiddāpadosika* (Delightful Play) who is skilled at preaching the Dharma."
For the sake of those celestial hosts, he then spoke these verses:
"Those with sensual desire are never satisfied; The person free from such causes has a mind that is content.
To give rise to a heart of dissatisfaction— Such is the death of ignorance."
The realms of all sentient beings, In their forms and types, are manifold;
Throughout the vast expanse of time, They have been unable to cultivate skillful means.
Forever denied peace and happiness, They are certain to fall into saṃsāra.
"Constantly dwelling in hell, birth after birth shall be likewise.
"If one were to speak the truth, the realm of Śakra is more wealthy, noble, and distinguished than that of the other devas."
One cannot escape this cycle of saṃsāra;
impermanence is certain and universal even among the gods. There is no subtle realm where one may avoid impermanence, for all must eventually fall.

At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, who was well-versed in the characteristics of phenomena and served as the father of those gods, exerted various kinds of diligence and expounded many causal practices; yet the host of devas still did not attain awakening. Who among them could joyfully cultivate the practice of tranquility and remain far removed from the defilement of sin?
Only those who are utterly deluded and whose minds are attached to negligence fail to accept and uphold these instructions for a long and boundless duration.
How can they remain unaware?
Those foolish people delight in creating the causes of evil.
"In that future life, one will be destroyed by various evils; how could one not know that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of evil karma bind one?
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"If one practices for the benefit of others, providing them with bedding, food, drink, clothing, and so forth,"
Providing offerings and making sacrifices for the assembly of both high and low, they do not seek blessings or profit for themselves;
or rather, they observe their own selves: who is the master that acts?
When encountering adverse conditions, one meets karmic enemies who commit offenses; though they come with intent to deceive and oppress, one gives rise to true patience.
Through the patience that is free from signs, the wise observe clearly that there is ultimately no affliction or hardship of suffering.
There is only the present, a restless thing, that forms such a body;
yet this body does not abide for even a single moment, and its prime vigor is likewise so—what body, then, could it destroy?
Sentient beings are deluded and intoxicated; regarding their own wealth and possessions, they fail to create benefit and instead increase their sinful karma.
Disregarding instructions and failing to practice generosity, they do not enjoy anything in any place, while thieves and the like watch for opportunities to plunder and destroy them.
How does one protect and uphold it?
Though those riches are exquisite and wonderful, one discards them as if casting away grass or wood,
with a mind free from attachment.

Constantly practicing the salvation of impoverished and inferior sentient beings, free from defilement and attachment, they obtain the precepts of the seven assemblies in both this life and future lives.
The supreme savior, who guards people through the precepts, shall cause them to be born in the heavens with vast wisdom.
He is the bridge across saṃsāra, which is like a prison of illness and other afflictions, and is fraught with great peril and evil.
Reaching that firm and secure state, the further shore of nirvana, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is likened to carrying a load:
though the object is light and small, one travels a long distance without becoming weary.
If a person carries a burden, provided their evil karma is light and slight, they will traverse the world at great distance without sinking.
It is like a bird with two strong wings: it soars high into the void and can reach distant places with speed.
"If a person upholds the precepts and guards them with firm resolve, desiring rebirth in heaven, it shall be just like this.
Furthermore, there was a bird named Manifesting Suchness (Tathatā) who dwelt on that White Mountain; being able to observe clearly, he spoke in verse:
"Just as my physical form does not abide for even a single moment, so too is happiness."
Fools are deluded and lack awakening.
If all types of beings possess many kinds of auspicious signs, they will certainly be destroyed at the time of rebirth within saṃsāra.
That merit is destroyed, and so it is for this life; when the King of Death finds his opportunity, how can one with a sinful mind escape?
Constantly practicing happiness, yet lacking wealth, one is bound by the Black Rope hell;
it crushes sentient beings, yet those who are strong and free from illness remain far removed from such suffering.
The King of Death draws near; as he approaches, the mind becomes deluded. The lives of all beings are destroyed, and their transgressions remain for a long time.
Gods and humans revolve in saṃsāra, unaware that their faculties are deluded. Far removed from peace and happiness, they fall into the realm of Yama, only then realizing the fruits of their karma.
In moments of pleasure, the body decays; one delights in sensory objects without realizing their attachment.
When the experience of pleasure is exhausted, the King of Old Age and Death invades; as the sense faculties encounter their objects, craving remains insatiable.
If there is no lamp of wisdom to illuminate and perceive the realm of sensory objects, one will experience and act within those spheres while clinging to the self through discrimination;
delighting in and adhering to the false, the fire of desire is constantly reborn.
The power of sensory objects is like the wind, Blowing the fire of desire to blaze. When wisdom awakens to True Suchness (*tathatā*), Conceptual thought becomes delusion.
All who are ignorant and confused Play about without awareness; Constantly moving within the realm of objects, They fan the flames of desire.

Devas and humans who indulge in sensual desires fall from that celestial realm; though they possess celestial virtues and truly enjoy celestial pleasures, when the signs of decay appear before them, how can they avoid destruction? Where shall they go?
Not abiding for even a single moment, arising and ceasing with every thought-instant, dwelling but briefly and not for long—such is that life.
This realm belongs to others; unaware of this with a single mind, one is swiftly parted from the blissful music of the Five Virtue Heaven through the suffering of decay.
The defilements of the three obstructions are stilled; taking refuge in the Triple Gem, the three karmas become vast and clear.
Awakening to the supreme state, one attains the Bodhi of the Three Buddhas.
Though born in a land of transgression, one is unsullied by the stains of sin, remaining focused on performing good deeds.
There, the wardens of Yama spoke these verses for those sentient beings:
"With a mind harboring greed, You spurned virtuous conditions; Failing to leave saṃsāra behind, You have obtained this bitter fruit.
Not relying on celestial conduct, You created the causes of your transgressions."
When one later encounters impermanence and regrets having committed evil, though one's body be cut by a sharp blade or one's person scorched by a fierce fire, it is still not as grievous as that.
Suffering is unbearable; when the eye beholds beautiful forms, one perceives pleasure as it truly is, yet how could one know that it is constant suffering?
Hearing sounds and indulging in flavors, the fault is likewise the same: one creates enemies through the commission of evil deeds.
Therefore, abandon those three enemies; they bind the sinner,
destroy his peace and happiness, and through the union of greed and delusion,
one distances oneself from the categories of virtue and falls into hell because of it.
If one practices the precepts, one will later obtain merit and goodness;
if one violates the precepts, one will later encounter affliction.
Drinking alcohol, taking life, violating another’s wife, holding wrong views, and double-tongued speech—
Failing to maintain dignified deportment, they indulge their passions and become dissolute; by destroying sentient beings, they sink into the evil realms.
Clinging greedily to perverse conduct and further uttering harsh words, they shall find no peace or happiness in this life or the next.
Stay far away from evil people and draw near to virtuous friends; thus extinguish these roots of sin.
If one does not believe in this karma, one will not obtain the fruits of karma, nor will there be any peace or happiness for the multitude.
The root of evil fruits is the afflictions that burn later.
If one utters false speech, though originally not a Dharma teacher claiming, "I understand the profound Dharma," they will later encounter impermanence and obtain the karmic fruit of Māra;
having turned from this human body, they shall be born in the evil realms.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that this ignorance and all craving—how can one obtain happiness?
By being content and free from greed, the body is liberated from afflictions.
To desire the arising of pleasure is itself called pleasure;
when conjoined with liberation, one attains the supreme bliss.
If one craves such pleasure, it is like water mixed with poison.
The bliss of liberation is like milk mixed with water; yet the fire of desire burns and harms, and the ignorant and blind do not perceive it.
Furthermore, they crave and covet wealth and profit; though they sell wine and meat and acquire countless riches, their minds remain unsatisfied.
The ghost of impermanence swiftly comes to drag one away.
If you indulge in sensual pleasures and delight in dwelling within sensory realms, you shall find no true happiness.
The Tathāgata has taught this through the analogy of awakening from a dream, like a city of *gandharvas*, or like empty space—devoid of reality.
Like bubbles upon the water;
like the core of a plantain tree;
like that fire-poison—so too are the objects of desire.
If one understands the causes and effects of flavors, perceives the faults and transgressions of desire, does not become deluded regarding true suchness (tathatā),
achieves wisdom, and attains tranquil contemplation; then,
having abandoned craving and attachment, suffering and affliction will not arise.
Like worldly poisons, their minds find no satisfaction; they fall from the celestial realms and descend again into hell.
Desiring to deceive the deluded, [sensual pleasures] are like a cascading torrent and like a flash of lightning.
The poisonous power of the world cannot surpass the allure of women; when thoughts of desire increase, they blaze like a raging fire.
One who is detached from desire attains tranquility—without before or after, and without middle—proceeding in accordance with suchness.
Growth is likewise so; they encounter the suffering of desire like a great blazing flame.
Knowing such faults, the wise remain far removed from it; by swiftly departing from desire, they will certainly attain peace and happiness.
The *nayuta* of devas, because of their sensual conduct, fall into the hell of fire and poison;
there they are punished with weapons and implements, its venom like fire, far removed from happiness.
Not engaging in the causes of desire, as in the aforementioned hells, one neither sees nor hears them.
If a person of greedy desire cuts off that craving for desire, they likewise will have no suffering or affliction.
Therefore, being stainless and having attained purity of mind,
one extinguishes the flames of desire in all places; entering into those various forms of supreme wholesome karma,
that practice remains untainted.
At that time, Śakra observed the bird perched upon the adorned tree, its color like refined gold.
Reflecting upon the causes and effects of that dharma—namely, right view and wholesome karma—he spoke these verses:
“Right view and wholesome karma are like that great tree, Lush and flourishing with a golden hue.”
Various adornments are described by the wise, arising everywhere like the ripening of good fruits.
Whether through unwholesome or wholesome deeds, one who has obtained this human body and further practices virtuous actions will be reborn in the heavens.
Falling into the hells below, one’s good intentions are deluded by desire, and thus one fails to obtain the supreme,
excellent medicine.
If one understands the retribution of actions, the mind will not cherish desire.
The realm of sentient beings is one of delusion, intoxication, and attachment; if greed is constantly practiced, evil will certainly arise together with it.
When afflictions arise in women, they are like the fire of the world; once this fire has arisen, afflictions are just like it.
Giving rise to thoughts of sentient beings, destroying the world, and causing all dharmas to perish—
these are the causes for hell.
Sweet in speech but poisonous at heart, with unstable affections and fleeting attachments, they are momentary in their love.
Their abandonment and turning away are likewise so.
Their nature is frivolous and restless, comparable to a flash of lightning; they deceive sentient beings while feigning acts of kindness and affection.
Their retinues consist of devas, humans, nāgas, ghosts, and rākṣasas, and their realms are likewise such.
Like that black poison, it makes no distinction of lineage and disregards one's power;
its love and hatred are inconsistent, and its nature is like wind or fire.
It seeks only wealth and possessions, utterly lacking any sense of beginning or end; when faced with danger and difficulty, it abandons and flees.
In this way, that wealthy man is loved and cherished; yet if he dwells in poverty and lowliness, they quickly depart from him.
It is like a wandering bee: when flowers are fragrant, it comes in competition to gather and feed upon them; but when the tree is withered and decayed, everyone stays far away.
The same applies to those without wealth; they are far removed from women.
Women are darkness, their minds are unrestrained and deranged; they destroy superior causes and know nothing of goodness.
As is the bondage of women, so too is the bondage of the gods;
if one encounters the bondage of women, one is certain to fall into hell. If one craves the beauty of women, it is the foremost among all cravings.
If there are sentient beings who, though they understand the nature of desire and karma, still remain attached to them, they are therefore ignorant; these deluded people do not awaken.
Feigning the expression of a sincere heart, they delude others while believing themselves to be trustworthy;
though their bodies dwell together, their minds are vastly different, and they bring harm to sentient beings.
Their venom is like that of snakes and scorpions; through various expedients, they seek much and nurture all things.
Women practice virtue, yet they cannot achieve it;
such is their inherent nature, utterly beyond measure. The wise do not cling to it, for their minds are ever resolute.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is the Sudharmā Hall.
At that time, the devas were assembled in the Sudharmā Hall.
To those who were thus distracted, a bird spoke this verse:
"For example, like birds, according to their own natures, there are two kinds who differ in what they find pleasant or loathsome:
some, upon seeing a lotus flower, take pleasure in it and become attached to it; others, upon seeing a forest or wild field, feel weary of it and seek to leave."
Upon first seeing a forest grove, one desires to dwell there with joy; yet, as if seeing a lotus flower, one then contemplates departing from it.
Sentient beings are likewise: the forest is like tranquil goodness, while the flower is a metaphor for sensual craving.
The wise delight in the forest, finding therein profound contentment.
The devas and humans are inverted, seeking instead the lotus flower.
Just as the emergence of the warm sun can dispel the great cold, so too is the bliss of liberation.
Suffering arises from craving; when pleasure fades, how can there be peace?
The wise do not delude themselves, but seek liberation; in all places, this constitutes the supreme bliss.
Dwelling in the grove of the Muni, one is able to observe skillfully, abiding with a mind free from greed.
The supreme among gods and humans dwell here in desire and greed, yet not for long.
If one practices non-greed, it is the highest among pleasures; dwelling in the seclusion of the forest is the foremost among practices.
All suffering is severed; one experiences the bitter fruits of evil conduct which deceive and delude sentient beings.
Regarding the delightful forests and mountains, one should observe them well;
with a mind that observes well, one dwells constantly in peace and happiness. With a mental disposition free from greed, one finds joy in the forest wilds.
That person delights in the forest; their mind is ever purely good. Free from desire and without greed, they attain the bliss of tranquility.
If a person is afflicted by defilements, they see the forest with fear; their craving increases all the more, and they burn themselves.
Having cast off craving and attachment, stainless and pure, with a mind settled in every birth, one constantly attains peace and happiness;
yet like one possessed of wealth and nobility, when merit is exhausted, it becomes empty.
In the prime of youth, old age swiftly encroaches; all that is loved is certain to be parted from.
All conditioned things are but temporary unions—this is the law of the world, rightly awakened and rightly taught.
If one awakens from folly and delusion, abandons craving, and practices contentment, entering the forest of tranquility, one shall obtain the supreme bliss.
But those who boast of their own cleverness and skill, whose thoughts and desires are manifold, depart far from the grove of goodness and forever lose benefit and joy.
Observing in silence amidst the forest, one attunes to stillness; with a contented mind free from greed, the virtuous heart reaches fulfillment.
Therefore, in the village, distraction arises constantly.

If you dwell in the mountain forests, free from all craving and attachment, your mind will swiftly grow weary of delusion; the supreme, tranquil forest is the dwelling place where you should abide in accordance with the Dharma.
If the activities of the mind are tranquil, one is forever free from afflictions; if one's conduct is in accord with the Way, the roots of goodness flourish and increase.
Even if someone were to obtain the status of a thousand Śakras, when their karmic lifespan ends, they too must return to birth and extinction.
Constantly practicing desire, one sees nothing at all; Subdued by desire, one gives rise to manifold sufferings.
The pleasure of sensual craving lasts but a fleeting moment; Before long, it perishes.
The mind is like an enemy; it can cause one to abandon that happiness, and such desire cannot be attained.
The bitter fruits of affliction all arise from desire; liberation gives rise to happiness, and that happiness is real.
In the conduct of the Sugata, acting with spontaneous accord, free from desire and greed, one attains inexhaustible bliss.
The pleasures of the five senses are sweet at first but bitter in the end; when the appearance of pleasure perishes, one sinks into hell.
The virtue of non-attachment—in its beginning, middle, and end—is stainless and pure;
it brings inexhaustible happiness and is the true mother of all goodness.
Deluded by sensual pleasures, how can one leave them behind?
Faults arise constantly, and there is profound suffering in the interim and thereafter.
How is it that through sinful deeds one does not see happiness?
There is a poisonous flower, its color brilliant and vibrant;
its substance is toxic, and if a person touches the flower, it harms their body.
The poison of sensual pleasure resulting from sinful deeds is likewise.
Furthermore, it is like grasping a torch against the wind;
it is also like a moth casting itself into the flame of a lamp.
So too does the fire of sensual desire burn and bring harm.
Therefore, the poison of desire must always be kept far away.
Because the gods are attached to desire, they accumulate evil in vain; humans are driven by craving and greed, their folly filling them with sinful deeds.
Therefore, the fire of desire burns away the roots of goodness, deceiving and causing one to lose the realms of gods and humans, sinking them into these evil destinies.
Before life has departed, quickly turn the mind back toward all that is wholesome and cultivate it so that it increases.
Greedy afflictions and delusions, the three transgressions giving rise to dust, and the three poisons acting as one—the net of sin remains vast.
Song, dance, and singing girls satisfy the ears and eyes according to desire; yet the will of Heaven is like stone.
Yet they are pulled and dragged by them.
All objects of desire shroud the tranquil mind; submerged in the river of craving, there is no time when one may cross over to liberation.
How deluded are you, O Deva, wishing to deceive me without realizing it?
It is like a poisonous tree that puts forth its toxic flowers; when bees and moths come to feed upon them, they perish by the poison.
The poison of greed causes harm in the same way; one falls into the three miserable realms as fire consumes wood.
Gods and humans remain unaware, being born into this land of sin; only when their suffering is exhausted shall they finally leave the hells.
Devas and humans are deluded and ignorant; they do not contemplate performing good deeds. In the realm of sin and evil, they possess not a single trace of faith.
The wise observe with discernment that all is truly like an illusion or a dream, yet fools do not perceive it as a dream, and thus create the causes for hell.
Therefore, by abandoning desire, one attains the excellence of liberation; by turning away from evil conduct, one cultivates the causes of benefit.
If that benefit is practiced, one will forever leave all evils behind; thus, in heaven, there are no dark deeds.
“That wise person, possessing right view and certainty, does not delight in distraction and shall obtain manifold blessings.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed the devaputra to practice non-distraction, and spoke in verse:
“The palaces of gods and humans are the root of distraction; one who is deluded, intoxicated, and attached [to them]...”
And thus one falls into saṃsāra.
If one is free from distraction, one is liberated even from saṃsāra.
That root of distraction is none other than ignorance, which is by nature darkness.
Like a person without eyes, I observe their fault:
they are deluded by fire and cannot distinguish it; their ignorance is deep and vast, and their distraction is likewise.
Having accumulated wealth and treasures to nourish oneself, one scatters them once more and falls into the miserable realms.
Originally hoping to escape suffering and enjoy pleasant happiness, who would have known that life would end?
One undergoes great suffering and affliction; the pleasures gathered through desire disperse before long.
For all sentient beings, karma and lifespan are limited; youth lasts but a moment, and one shall soon grow old.
Bound by the fetters of good and evil karma, who can attain true sovereignty?
For example, as a puppeteer manipulates a wooden figure, it requires the aid of thread and string to perform its actions;
so too it is with sentient beings— they require the aid of afflictions and karma to remain within saṃsāra.
If one is free from craving and attachment, there will be no activity.
That which is not the long-term practice of karma is not believed by the wise;
one should remain far removed from all methods of distraction. If one is free from distraction, one will not be reborn within the three realms.
For example, suppose there were a person who fell down a deep precipice; yet among them, some might still survive without losing their lives.
But if a person is distracted and falls from the precipice of the triple world, there is none among them who can attain liberation.
Among all afflictions and karmic actions, distraction is the most grave; throughout day and night, one is never at peace.
For those in the world, even the slightest distraction destroys the intention for transcendence among sentient beings; therefore, one must distance oneself from it.
When the Blessed One had thus spoken the truth from his seat, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, conceived a heart of reverence.
He spread out his own seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and stood up with palms joined. Seeing the verses written there, fear arose in his mind, and he recited these stanzas:
“If one is not distracted, it is like that nectar;”
If one acts with distraction, one falls into impermanence.
One who is undistracted is the most supreme among gods.
Distracted conduct is the root of saṃsāra; pure conduct—
This is the root of peace and happiness.
Therefore, through right concentration, one attains the supreme bliss in all circumstances.
If one regards sensual pleasure as one would dread extreme suffering, then the great poison of distraction—which destroys all virtues like the poison of delusion—will be abandoned.
When a person practices wholesome deeds, they do not follow after distraction and can attain peace and happiness.
If that wise one explains impartially that both virtue and non-virtue are rooted in the grasping at a self;
all such grasping is the root of suffering and pleasure.
"As for me, O World-Honored One, through these verses and scriptures, I have become free from desire and purified, attaining benefit and peace.
