Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Great Dharma Teacher Fǎtiān, a purple-robed śramaṇa and subject, by imperial decree, at Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India.
At that time, there was a bird named Adṛṣṭapūrva-darśana (Never-before-seen). As it moved without distraction, it spoke these verses:
“The minds of greed, hatred, and delusion are constant companions of transgression; they are the seeds of hell.
The hearts of greed, hatred, and delusion are those that perpetually commit offenses; they fall from the precipice of the three miserable realms.”
Only later does one realize that the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion cannot fail to cause fear;
therefore, the wise subdue them so as not to allow them to become distracted.
Drinking alcohol and speaking falsehoods, killing living beings and stealing, lacking faith in cause and effect,
harboring anger and committing evil deeds— failing to guard against these,
one will not be reborn in the heavens but will sink into the miserable realms.
Constantly practicing sensual desire, craving possesses great power; it enslaves sentient beings, causing them to be indolent and lazy, such that they never possess even a trace of virtue.
Furthermore, like clouds and mists obscuring the eye of wisdom, one commits many transgressions against the precepts;
even if one attains a human body, it will be of an inferior kind.
If the mind dwells in vice, it is boundless darkness;
if the mind dwells in awakening, it is like the great light of day.
Such are the various dharmas proclaimed by the Buddha.
Innate distraction is like being intoxicated by wine; because of that distraction, one wanders through the hells and transmigrates among humans, all of which lead to ruin and destruction.
Thus it is certain: birth is truly impermanent; with heavy obstacles of distraction, one falls into the ocean of sensory realms, thereby creating the causes for shackles and fetters.
The devas indulge much in play; when their birth is exhausted, their happiness is forever severed.
Their minds become distracted, they alter their roots of goodness, and though they are deeply attached to realms of pleasure, their hearts remain unsatisfied.
Devas and humans do not realize that this is the root of suffering and affliction; there is no time for negligence, not even for a moment, nor for the duration of a single kṣaṇa.
Not overcome by craving, with the realms of desire severed, one does not fail to awaken in a hundred ways.
Constantly enjoying celestial bliss, yet indulging in attachment and negligence, one is subdued by desire.
Just as the fires of hell incinerate sentient beings without making any distinction,
so too do the fires of desire incinerate the hosts of devas without making any distinction.
Furthermore, as with hungry ghosts, whose mouths emit flaming torches that burn their food and drink;
so too is it with the fires of hunger for those among the class of animals.
"Such is the fire of desire, which pervades the world and burns all things,
yet sentient beings do not perceive it.
There was a bird named Guḍhaguṇa (Endowed with Virtue) who, perceiving their distraction and the failure to practice what is wholesome, later fell from that heaven and spoke this verse:
"When wholesome karma is exhausted, this life lasts but a moment.
When sentient beings are disciplined, a person attains the supreme state.
All youth ends in an instant; life is brought to its close."
All wealth and nobility are destroyed in an instant.
Gods and humans are not permanent; wealth and nobility are not permanent. They do not abide for even a single kṣaṇa; do not harbor distracted thoughts.
Therefore, practice early, diligently cultivate what is beneficial, and guard the laws of restraint;
in the state of tranquil principle, the faults of defilement do not arise—O Deva, why do you not see this?
If the mind is distracted, the practice of the Dharma will not be constant; once gone, there is no returning, and so it is with happiness.
By guarding the root of the precepts, one attains the joy of devas and humans.
If those sentient beings lack this precept, they will inevitably suffer affliction later.
Therefore, practicing the conduct of the precepts in this manner at all times is the most supreme among all forms of happiness.
Those whose precepts are pure attain great fruit;
fools who lack precepts are not born in the heavens.
Amidst the objects of the five desires, they experience pleasure, yet their minds do not reflect upon them.
All things are impermanent;
their lives are destroyed. Countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of devas, deluded by desire and distracted, are cast into the fires of the five sensual pleasures and consumed by them.
All forms of distraction are what people delight in and cling to; yet they are impermanent in the end, and one only realizes this when the fruit is reaped.
When agitation reaches its peak, it is great suffering; having encountered suffering, one sees the delusion, for the mind clings to objects of attachment and remains unaware of its own anguish.
Suffering and affliction continue to arise, leading to regret later on.
Defilements and doubts are born from sensory objects; my mind being ignorant, it performs the actions of saṃsāra.
That wheel of saṃsāra follows the human mind; through mutual delusion, beings wander on and on within the three realms.
When the wise realize the truth, they see that saṃsāra abides as impermanent, suffering, and empty; thus, that suffering does not truly exist.
If one is addicted to female beauty and constantly practices lustful defilement, they shall not later behold the realms of the devas.
To practice what is contrary to the Dharma is the most extreme among evils.
In all the worlds, there is no other savior; only the True Dharma exists.
Therefore, rely upon the Dharma.
If one is estranged from the Dharma, people will delight in what is contrary to the Dharma.
Once unrighteousness has been committed, the fires of suffering blaze forth, and one is forever severed from the celestial realms.
When wholesome karma is utterly exhausted, one falls down without even realizing it;
reflecting on that former happiness, one finds it is impermanent and no longer exists. Bound by the cords of karma, who can find peace and joy?
"Craving increases further, dragging them into the evil realms, forever separated from the heavens.
At that time, Śakra, seeing the various celestial hosts receiving hundreds of kinds of merit and fortune, was greatly struck with awe and fear, and immediately spoke in verse:
"Performing good brings happiness; the gods receive the rewards of goodness, which is the supreme cause for being among gods and humans."
Having performed wholesome deeds in the past, like the sun traveling through the sky,
they illuminate the world with a single,
non-dual halo; likewise, the light of their wisdom illuminates the darkness of error, and is likewise without duality.
Desiring to go to the celestial palaces, one practices the conduct of compassion; by bestowing compassion upon all living beings, one becomes their mother who gives birth to them.

Relying on this goodness, people are born in the heavens. Furthermore, through a heart of compassion that brings benefit, profit, and joy to all sentient beings, one attains the cherished delights of the gods.
The compassionate one is ever virtuous; all sentient beings, as well as the worthy and the holy, universally take refuge in him.
Furthermore, he practices compassion like the cool moon, removing the heat of afflictions and the suffering of burning flames.
Therefore, the compassionate mind is the root of happiness; it is the master of all desires for the lords of gods and humans.
Regarding forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, it never finds enough to grasp upon.
The bhikṣu observed and spoke in verse: "Just as when the kalpa is destroyed,
and the fires of the sun blaze fiercely, the great oceans and rivers are all completely dried up."
Even after passing through ten million, a hundred thousand, and ten thousand kalpas, the ocean of greed, delusion,
and desire cannot be exhausted.
A person’s greedy mind surpasses even that of a dragon.
The cause of distraction gives rise to all evils. Do not practice distraction;
the fault of distraction exceeds that of any person, for it obstructs the principle of True Suchness (tathatā).
If one practices distraction, they will never possess goodness.
Separated from all pleasure, not born in the celestial realms, with life constantly arising and ceasing as the root of agitation—
the mind understands this to be the supreme among sufferings.
If one does not understand that the preceding faculties and objects are cyclic existence, yet clings to them as being determinate;
they are like flowers in the sky, like the city of the Gandharvas, like bubbles on water,
and like masses of foam.
Deluded by those masses of foam, they take them for bedding and such;
deluded by those magical illusions, they take them as their own gathered movements.
So too it is with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and garuḍas—they are all likewise illusory.
Who can save one from impermanence?
If one merely performs actions without fearing in time, the most evil King of Death will swiftly come to oppress and harm.
Therefore, perform wholesome deeds so that later there will be no afflictions; I awaken you all: do not act with negligence!
They give rise to craving again and are dragged away by sensory objects;
these objects bind sentient beings like heavy shackles and chains, serving as the cause for hell and leading them forever away from liberation.
Therefore, that which is unreal you must distance yourself from;
this true Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One—listen attentively and practice it, and you will gain inexhaustible benefit.

At that moment, Śakra suddenly beheld the image of the Buddha; together with the hosts of devas, he conceived a heart of reverence, prostrated himself with his head at the feet [of the Buddha], and spoke in verse:
“That Blessed One, the World-Honored One, The Truly All-Knowing One, Manifests the form of a savior, Skillfully opening the way to liberation.”
If one takes refuge and pays homage, one is liberated from saṃsāra and the mind attains supreme goodness;
this well-disciplined state is stainless and pure.
The Buddha taught this Dharma, which accomplishes the path to Nirvana; he said that the practitioner who follows it attains the power of fearlessness,
experiences the bliss of cessation, dwells on the ground of true emptiness,
and crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having crossed the perils of the three realms, you have opened the eye of wisdom and emitted the most supreme light, seeing the entire world.
You are not like the common and ignorant, who are as inert as earth or wood, lacking such radiance and wandering through delusive realms.
If a person is defiled by the stain of greed, their mind is not pure; the faults of speech are like poisons.
Yet, by means of the water of wisdom, they may wash away these stains and leave behind all attachment.
Holding to the notion of a self and being ignorant, you were unable to see this truth;
now that stainless speech shall be explained for you.
When the Buddha was on the path of practice, he did not engage in distraction, yet he rescued and delivered you all;
now that he has reached the other shore, he further delivers others, bringing benefit and happiness to all within this world.
The Buddha alone abides; taking no-gain as gain is the supreme benefit for others.
Thus, by committing evil, one falls into the great hells;
thus, by cultivating goodness, one shall be born in the heavens.
At that time, Śakra, observing the assembly of devas, spoke these verses: "Just as a bird,
when driven by a swift wind, Is carried along in its flight, So too do humans and devas revolve in their coming and going,
All brought about by the influence of karma."
Just as suffering and pleasure arise through aggregation and perish through disintegration, so too does their meaning follow the excellence or inferiority of karma.
Therefore, all conditioned formations constitute cause and effect.
The Muni has declared:
"Tathatā is boundless and the basis of equality; the seeds of karmic habituation are produced by all minds, yet they are difficult to subdue. Only the Buddha-Tathāgata [can do so]."
And thus they bring them to awakening.
From ten to a hundred, from a hundred to a thousand, up to nayutas of countless sentient beings—
of various kinds— all fallen into the great net of karma.
The world is like a painting by Zhuangzi; it is like a flying bird tethered by a cord:
though it wishes to soar into the void, in the end it cannot depart.
"Yet they create various karmas and are bound by those karmas; though they wish to escape saṃsāra, they cannot go forth.
At that time, Śakra saw the gods distracted, amusing themselves together and deeply attached to their pleasures; observing that host of devas, he spoke this verse:
"The five pleasures of song and dance pervade all of heaven; yet if one does not contemplate [their impermanence], one will certainly fall.
You crave women, clinging to them by your very nature, never for a moment letting go."
The minds of others are not constant; they advance or retreat according to their own whims.
The wealthy are loved and constantly obtain wealth and goods; yet when one feigns intimacy and pleases them, if they appear stubbornly stingy, they will lightly abandon and distance themselves.
Chasing after sensual pleasures is like a thirsty deer that rushes toward a mirage in competition with others,
seeking water; indulgence in desire is likewise empty, false, and unreal.
Those women have neither gratitude nor righteousness; they distinguish neither the distant from the near, nor do they regard noble or humble birth.
For example, like a wandering bee that, when it encounters flowers in full and fragrant bloom, immediately gathers and consumes their nectar;
yet if it sees withered flowers, it immediately abandons them and departs.
Furthermore, women are deceitful and delusive; they are like honey within which a poisonous drug is hidden—so too is their harmful treachery.
The person of wisdom, with a mind upright and resolute, does not cling at all to these desires and delusions.
Like ants gathering at putrid meat, or like bees guarding honey, so do the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts [cling].
All the evil yakṣas, piśācas and the like, mātaras, ṛkṣas,
as well as rākṣasas, are likewise deluded.
The arising of delusive realms is like illusory phenomena; they deceive sentient beings, so that when impermanence arrives, one is unaware of their decay and destruction.
All these forest trees, adorned with flowers and fruits, act as the ropes of birth and death that bind you;
like a calf tethered by a rope, you lack all autonomy.
In the realm of happiness, with one's male and female kin, who can provide protection at the time of impermanence?
If a person dwells in the abode of wisdom born of much learning and virtuous karma— the supreme state of mental composure— I shall now depart.
In Jambudvīpa, springs, streams, rivers, and seas, as well as gardens, groves, pavilions, and terraces, are all fully present.
Regarding those things that do not accord with the Dharma, there is the wisdom of debating and studying the teachings, both what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
"I now know them all:
these false and hostile minds that delude and deceive sentient beings.
Then, another bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"The mind-enemy is base and inferior, giving rise to the poison of the five faculties;
it bites and stings sentient beings like a five-headed serpent, leaving one to harbor empty regret."
The five objects of the senses, such as form and the rest, constitute a great river of craving; none have reached its far shore.
That far shore is tranquil, free from all error and delusion.
False views bring no benefit; through delusion, one falls into hell.
Such people of false views conceive of non-causes as causes;
fallen into evil and perverse views, they shroud their tranquil minds. Misunderstanding cause and effect, they undergo the hardships of saṃsāra.
One obtains a body of suffering;
as the fruits of karma arise and perish, so too do good and evil.
If one perceives true emptiness, one immediately reaches the other shore and forever leaves behind arising and ceasing.
You should know this: the foolish are deluded by desire, and desire obscures and confuses those who are lost.
If one abides in right view—subtle, pure, and characterized by the restraint of ethical conduct—one will not find it difficult to attain the supramundane state or rebirth among the devas.
If one clings to false views and performs perverse, difficult practices—
praying for long life while further deluding others—
one's conduct will be shrouded in darkness, and one will fall into the great cycle of saṃsāra.
Accomplishing the causes of suffering, its nature is one of oppression.
As the Buddha taught:
"The essential means for benefit and joy is to reflect back upon the true nature; when the faculties, objects, and their spheres are empty,"
My mountain crumbles of itself; afflictions are purified. Having emerged from the perils of birth and death, I dwell in the city of Nirvana—this is true liberation.
All sentient beings are deeply attached to sensual pleasures; with poisonous delusions having entered their hearts, they can never reach the further shore of nirvana.
Even if for a hundred kalpas one were submerged in the world like one bound in shackles and unable to escape,
the wise have taught that by faithfully accepting and practicing the sublime scriptures— the wealth of the supramundane Dharma—
one will swiftly obtain great and wholesome benefit.
Stubbornly clinging to the inferior, they rely on false and deceptive scriptures;
deluded sentient beings fall everywhere into saṃsāra. How can these beings deceive the true Dharma?
"Seeing falsely without cause, they do not pity living beings; falling themselves and causing others to fall, both enter the evil realms.
There was a bird there named Madhukara, who, while eating honey and sporting in that grove of trees, spoke this verse:
“Sentient beings drink alcohol and are deluded and intoxicated; Who knows that they are dragged by the noose of ignorance through their craving for its flavor?
They fall into the impermanent and evil realms; Therefore, do not drink the wine of ignorance.”
The cause of saṃsāra arises from contact, giving birth to deluded views; all that is non-Dharma arises from craving.
The ocean of all afflictions and karma is deep—this is what the Tathāgata, with great wisdom, has taught.

You should know that drinking alcohol destroys name-and-form; like one who is blind, there is no distinction between good and evil, such that even when the body falls over, one remains unaware—this is a cause for the ridicule of others, comparable to wood or stone.
Drinking alcohol lacks constancy and brings many faults; thirty-six transgressions arise from it, leading to discord and violation.
For the wise, attachment is a great darkness; therefore, one should distance oneself from drinking alcohol.
The *kāśa* flower is as light as such a person—floating, fickle, and lacking in loyalty and faith.
It increases greed and hatred, perpetuating the cycle of birth and death; one must exert effort to subdue this power and provide diligent protection.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further spoke in verse:
“Non-anger overcomes anger; Patience overcomes enmity; The Dharma overcomes non-Dharma;
Light overcomes darkness.”
Truth destroys false speech; concentration destroys divisive talk; goodness destroys harsh words; and intimacy destroys estrangement.
Loving-kindness destroys killing; generosity destroys stinginess; mindfulness destroys unmindfulness; and wisdom destroys ignorance. Daylight destroys the night;
and the bright fortnight destroys the dark month.
False desires and discursive thoughts are shattered by true awakening wisdom;
the karma that leads to the miserable realms is shattered by the Eightfold Noble Path;
and the four unhindered knowledges shatter all dullness and incapacity.
Wisdom destroys ignorance and dwells in tranquility, destroying that which is grasped by clinging;
as wind destroys mountains and fire destroys all things, as the ocean swallows rivers and the sun outshines the stars;
as wealth destroys poverty, fire destroys cold, and water destroys thirst.
Food overcomes hunger;
sufficiency overcomes insufficiency. One should always praise compassion and not praise the absence of compassion.
The evil karma of false speech causes sentient beings to fall into ruin.
Skillfully expounding True Suchness (tathatā) and shattering the wisdom of the conditioned, you are like the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
who can destroy the heterodox;
as the various powers of the devas destroy the asuras.
Śakra declared: "I have defeated you all, the entire host of devas. Why was this so?
Those who abide in the True Dharma possess such majestic power.
Were they to wander again through saṃsāra, even among the ranks of slaves, they would remain as if sleeping upon the earth,
dwelling always at the lowest level.
If one again focuses the single mind, practicing and upholding the True Dharma, it is like ascending a throne; one will be above all.
If one’s conduct is deluded regarding wisdom and one delights in practicing what is not the Dharma, then by the natural fruit of one’s own karma, where could one go without falling?
Blown by the winds of karma, they revolve through the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal kingdom—
who could share in their suffering on their behalf?
As for all those who are ignorant and deluded, all sentient beings who create evil karma for themselves...

Sentient beings in saṃsāra gather and disperse according to their karma; they are likewise unstable.

Just as when it rains from heaven, the rain does not abide in the void;
so too is happiness, for it does not abide in the illusory body.
Just as a great wind blows away the clouds and thunder;
Pleasure is likewise; it blows away one's life.
Like rotten wood falling into a great flame, it can never return to its former state.

That which was taught by the seven Buddhas is that precepts and concentration are foremost; through constant mindfulness, one attains the stage of human karma in every birth.
"Reflecting upon many kalpas, through the karmic ground of my parents, I have attained birth in the heavens.
At that time, Śakra spoke again in verse:

Now, having observed all the precepts, one is reborn in the heavens.
Birth among humans is difficult to obtain; even for those who do obtain it, it is like casting a needle into a mustard seed.
If one is deluded or distracted, one will fall again into hell.
Having practiced the three types of wholesome action, one should observe the mind with tranquility and discernment;
thus afflictions will naturally be eliminated, and one will certainly be reborn in the heavens.
By subduing and exhausting the afflictions, a sense of inner joy and satisfaction arises.
Pure and free from greed and hatred, one attains birth in the heavens.
Having severed both aversion and attachment, great suffering does not arise;
by further practicing various acts of giving, one attains birth in the heavens.
Constantly exercising a mind of compassion to rescue and protect all sentient beings,
as one would protect one's own life, one will be born in the heavens.
To act otherwise with an unwholesome mind and harm others is as poisonous as fire.
Bestowing whatever is requested, one attains birth in the heavens. If,
upon seeing another’s wife or concubine, one does not give rise to a mind of lustful defilement,
but regards her with reverence and affection as one would a mother, one attains birth in the heavens.
If one regards false speech as fire arising from the tongue,
and if one's observance of the precepts is genuine, one will be reborn in the heavens.
By refraining from divisive speech, one brings friends and kin into harmony.
Loving speech eliminates estrangement, and one thereby attains birth in the heavens.
Harsh words spoken without restraint wound others like a blade;
good speech puts an end to prior faults, and one thereby attains birth in the heavens.
Idle chatter increases transgressions, as do elaborate and flowery words;
Speaking in accordance with reason and truth leads to rebirth in the heavens.
One should maintain and protect this precept, which was proclaimed by the seven Buddhas alike.
When the fearless discipline of the Dharma is perfected, one attains rebirth in the heavens.
Yet all sentient beings, if they give rise to overweening pride,

At that time, a certain bhikṣu spoke this verse:
"If the rope of this woman binds a person most firmly,
when one undergoes retribution within saṃsāra, the evil fruit is foremost."
If this woman is a rope, it is not a rope for binding the neck;
it is that which binds the hearts of sentient beings, producing suffering as its primary function.
The woman’s rope binds men with such intensity that there is nothing in the human world to compare with it.
Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—these are led away, bound by that woman.
A great cord of physical form binds the body; one can perceive the dimensions of this cord’s shape.
But the cord of the woman’s mind is not physical; it binds the great [self] yet possesses no form or dimension.
Though the woman’s rope may be pleasing to the mind, it binds all people in delusion so that they find no liberation; they do not emerge from the perils of saṃsāra.
While all six sense-objects bind man, the power of the woman’s rope is greatest.
Among those who subdue sentient beings, this bond is supreme.
If one is bound by such a woman— her foolish and deluded mind full of attachment—
she becomes a wife, concubine, or kinswoman, a firm and unbreakable fetter.
Thus, that Lord Śakra and all one thousand of these devaputras saw [him].
Their hearts were filled with joy; they danced, sang, and offered praise to the Heavenly King, speaking in verse:

Practicing the sublime conduct of Brahmā among the devas, one is not attached to sensual pleasures;

Harmonizing the mind with the Dharma—such bliss has never existed before.
Supreme and most excellent wisdom, truthful words born of a compassionate mind,
the Dharma of happiness is impermanent, pure and untainted.
All worldly virtues, as well as those supramundane virtues—

as karma is superior, middling, or inferior, so too is the fruit it evokes.

Women are fickle in nature; their guiles are manifold, and they cannot be restrained.

She shares no wealth or profit with him, nor does she draw near to him; though their natures and behaviors differ, her mind can conceive of greatness.

Like a flower on a snake, like the fleshly heart of a woman, like fire covered by ashes—so too is the veil of beauty.
Pleasing yet unwholesome, the body is like a poisonous tree that produces those poisonous flowers; do not draw near it.
Constantly intent upon sensual objects and attached to women, people find no happiness in this life or the next.

Of all forms of discipline, the discipline of women is foremost; why not leave women?

The bonds of those women, fierce fires, and weapons cannot burn or cut; the powerful strength of sentient beings cannot be subdued.

These eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not abide within their respective objects:

like the inherent nature of fire, which can burn grass and wood, when could it ever have enough?
The fire of those six sense-faculties, wavering and indecisive, burns these sentient beings until they possess no awareness at all.
This ground of distraction is where the Dharma is not practiced;
by departing from that distraction and its cherished objects, a person follows their own karma and attains abiding in reality.
When women give rise to love, their minds are difficult to restrain; according to the causes of their own karma, they experience separation in existence.

Therefore, one should always distance oneself from this great poison of desire.

Women, driven by craving, fall into the greatest transgression, for they possess no resolute mind.

as the earth and the wind differ in their movement and stillness, so too do the kindness and harm of women differ.

It is like a heron or a magpie, standing and gazing at a dried-up pond.

So it is with women: true love has never been seen. Birth [in this world] is a net of faults, obstructing the Dharma of humans.
Just as sunlight is inseparable from the sun’s essence, so too is that deceitful affection inseparable from women.

With a mind joyful and peaceful, abandon hardships; if a single thought of transgression arises, one quickly forgets kindness.
Difficult to subdue, it is like fire; one should swiftly abandon it, seeking the wondrous bliss of tranquility by withdrawing into the mountain forests.
When devas conceive such thoughts, they are deluded by sensual pleasures; failing to realize the terrors of evil, they will surely suffer the loss of their lives and lifespans.
Though born in those heavens, impermanence is certain, like the sun setting at night.

He has encountered impermanence, the greatest of evil states;

With distraction as its root, first subdue the proliferation of discursive thoughts; thereafter, eliminate impermanence.
Attaining the bliss of the life of Dharma—this is said to be supreme.
This non-distraction can lead one to the heavenly realms; by skillfully understanding the bonds of suffering, liberation likewise follows.

Untainted by sinful dharmas, their spheres of experience are likewise so; free from all fetters and the paths of saṃsāra, they are equal to refined gold.
Dwelling neither in defilement nor dust, they emerge from the perils of birth and death, becoming entirely pure.
When the six sense faculties do not engage with their objects, defiled phenomena do not arise;

Deluded regarding all phenomena— both what is beneficial and what is not— such a person lacks merit and remains far removed from Nirvana.
By drawing near to the Dharma Master, one attains true knowledge of the Dharma; practicing the Dharma, one seeks its fruit.
Thus accomplished, the mind is ever free from delusion; with all faculties subdued, one reaches the further shore.
The mind seeks but finds no rest, entangled within its objects; the wise are able to eliminate this, acting as teachers of the Dharma for the sake of the world.
In the gardens of the heavens, one sports with sovereign ease, obtaining much joy and delight in realms of pleasure.
If one can renounce [these] and perform those wholesome deeds, the mind will be tranquil and at peace.
This is most difficult: to be born in the realm of Yāma.
Those who are born in that heaven through false conceptualization number in the tens of millions (*koṭi*) and even the hundreds of billions (*paduma*), having obtained the fruits of their own karma.
If the mind is difficult to tame, it produces the fruits of those karmic actions;

driven by the mind, one revolves through the twelve links of dependent origination, circling in succession through the past, present, and future, among humans and gods. All sentient beings are created solely by the mind.
At the summit of Mount Sumeru is a ground of lapis lazuli, where Śakra and the holy sages dwell eternally.
There is another peak composed of lapis lazuli where the gandharvas reside; humans cannot reach it.
Forests and groves, scattered and situated apart, delight the mind;
no human can reach them.
Upon the supreme golden ground, there are lotus ponds made of lapis lazuli; no human can reach them.
And there are various ponds and pools where flocks of birds gather;
they come and go in play, most exquisite and supreme, such that humans cannot reach them.
Palaces and vehicles, most excellently adorned—herein dwell the devas, while humans remain far removed.
Because humans are so remote, they are deceived by the objects of desire; thus, though worldly suffering exists, their minds feel no fear.
Becoming ever more ignorant and stubborn, they continue to wander through saṃsāra.
Constantly undergoing manifold sufferings, like being bound by ropes or like a bird confined in a cage,
they are unable to be reborn in any of those various, sublime celestial realms above.
The bonds of worldly women destroy wholesome dharmas and increase birth and death.
If a person is greedily attached to them, they will be assailed and destroyed by the armies of the Lord of Death as they compete to overwhelm him.
The nature of distraction is to be deludedly attached to women; when the time of impermanence arrives, one must personally experience the fruits of one's own karma.
Since they are merely objects for play, why cherish women? You will certainly obtain them [in the future].
Birth and death are great afflictions;
constantly craving fame and profit, one incurs suffering in the same way.
Bound by those women, one creates much greed and attachment, which is difficult to subdue.
Yet it constitutes a great affliction, harming and injuring all sentient beings in the world.
If this bond of a woman were the only one, then the craving for worldly desires would be the greatest of faults.
Reflecting with single-minded focus, he knew that his transgression was indeed as it was; since the fault of desire was so deep, how could he avoid falling?
All those people who subdue their minds, leave desire behind, and distance themselves from women are born in the Yāma Heaven.
Like the sun, like the stars, they illuminate wherever they go; riding through the void with ease and joy, all things are likewise so.
This radiance is fully possessed by devas and humans; everything is thus.
The Lord of Devas, seeing that the assembly had grasped at signs and become attached to that radiance, proclaimed verses in golden letters, speaking in verse as follows:
“The celestial body is free from impurity and grease; By constantly practicing pure conduct, One does not allow distraction to arise, And shall long obtain happiness.”
Neither pleasure nor pain is spared; neither the old, the young, nor those in their prime;
neither the high-born nor the low-born—none escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether they have a master or no master, whether they possess strength or lack it, none are exempt.
Whether ugly or handsome, one cannot escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether a king or a minister, whether lay or ordained,
whether virtuous or non-virtuous, none can escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether noble or poor, virtuous or lacking virtue,
whether in a female or male body, none can escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether in the wilderness or the mountains, in the water or on the land— none are spared.
Masters, servants, birds, and beasts— none escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether sleeping or awake, whether eating or fasting—
all who dwell in this world cannot avoid being destroyed by the King of Death.
Whether on earth or in the heavens, in this world or in other realms,
the cycle of transmigration is likewise such that one cannot escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether possessing great merit or meager merit, whether fierce and strong or gentle and mild— none are exempt.
Whether afflicted by illness or dwelling in physical well-being, none can escape destruction by the King of Death.
Whether among hungry ghosts or animals, humans or non-humans alike,
being powerless and incapable, how could one possibly avoid destruction by the King of Death?
In the realm of desire and the realm of form, all devas and humans dwell;
yet when their merit and lifespan are exhausted, none can escape destruction by the King of Death.
Even reaching up to the formless realm, all the hosts of devas—
Though one dwells in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), one cannot escape destruction by the King of Death.
All things within the three realms, whether sentient or insentient, are like illusions and transformations;
only those who have transcended the world and severed all fetters are not invaded by that King of Death.
Knowing the power of this impermanence, all sensual desires arise;
one falls and undergoes saṃsāra, revolving without end.
By relishing the objects of the world, afflictions are produced because of desire.
Violating and harming others is like a venomous snake; one will sink forever into hell.
Sentient beings face the hardship of impermanence; though they wish to do good, they lack the power.
Wandering through the cycle of existence is entirely created by the mind.
Deluded by desire, they act with distraction; Delighting in the objects of the five sensory realms, The snares of craving bind gods and humans, Causing them to fall into the evil destinies.
Gods and humans act with distraction, Greedily craving all forms of pleasure.
Not abiding is like a cascading river; when the body falls, there is no awareness at all.
Those attached to that pleasure stand in danger of life as if on a precipice;
the celestial hosts cannot perceive them, like the blind treading upon a wrong path.
One who is deluded by desire and attached to pleasure is not like a blind man;
though the deluded fall into the three miserable realms, the blind man does not fall.
Therefore, acting out of desire is not even equal to being sightless.
Never satiated with sensual desires, how can one know that the mind is deluded?
Falling away without ever leaving the mind, one constantly performs deeds of no benefit.
Those who practice sensual craving possess neither wisdom nor knowledge.
In every thought-moment, the suffering of desire arises; why then do you still practice desire?
This fruit of desire that it brings forth is like finding an evil friend:
it drags one into the palace of impermanence and causes one to dwell forever in the miserable realms.
When a person dies, they do not return; like a flowing stream that never turns back, so too are sensual pleasures—all are but empty illusions.
The lives of all sentient beings arise and perish like bubbles upon the water.
The stream of youth does not turn back; it rushes away like a flowing river.
Birth, old age, impermanence, and suffering—all these exist in their entirety.
Gods and humans do not perceive this, for their minds are ever distracted.
If one gives rise to stainless wisdom and applies the mind to pure conduct,
one will easily obtain a human body in this world and never again enter the evil realms.
One shall cause unarisen virtues to arise and cause those already arisen to increase.
Whatever good one performs follows the mind, and the fruits of one's own actions are likewise so.
When a virtuous mind encounters the objects of desire, it views them as if looking upon a vessel, a staff, or poison;
yet when an unvirtuous mind clings to the objects of desire, it finds pleasure through delusion.
The faculties are either wholesome or unwholesome; all depend upon one’s own mind.
When the mind gives rise to the accumulation of afflictions, one obtains the fruits of good and evil.
The wise person observes correctly and perceives that form is equal and empty.
When the conditions for suffering and its origin are severed, how could there be separate fruits?
All blazing sensory objects arise from one’s own mind;
if the mind is well-tamed, it is equal to the emptiness of form.
Just as in a single sheaf of rice, the stalks and other parts differ in their color and form, so too it is with the activities of the mind (*citta-saṃskāra*): various afflictions arise.
That rice represents the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); the mind-king produces all mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
Just as rice produces distinct stalks and so forth, the worldly mind is likewise.
Distraction and desire for forms— wherein the realm of form is likened to drifting clouds—
one fails to perceive the arising of bitter fruits, yet revolves according to the marks of karma.
Having seen this suffering, what pleasure could gods or humans desire?
If one constantly gives rise to sensual craving, one distances oneself from all that is wholesome; therefore, the wise person abandons desire.
Suffering is in truth ever suffering and empty; this is the intrinsic characteristic of suffering.
Since the fruit of suffering is impermanent, it is not what the wise delight in.
The objective realm deceives the mind, and the mind, being deluded, engages in the karma of ignorance.
When devas fall from their celestial realms, they are dragged by karma without any awareness.
Even if one is born in the Yāma Heaven, one's own nature becomes illusory;
being foolish, blind, and lacking the eye of wisdom, one does not see the defilements of craving and pride.
"Having fallen, one encounters impermanence.
At that time, Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) spoke these verses:
"With the eye of awakening observing impermanence, The signs of decay burn oneself from within."
Even if one dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven, when retribution is exhausted, it is like a lamp going out.
The twelve links of great power form a wheel spread throughout the Dharma-realm;
when karma and retribution circulate, birth and extinction are each uncertain.
The Sutra on the Noble Foundations of Mindfulness, Fascicle Eight; the collection of verses in gāthā meter concludes.
